title: Mesopotamian Mythology: Figures, Relationships and Story Cycles
description: Three thousand years of Sumerian, Akkadian, Babylonian and Assyrian gods mapped as a relationship graph: the mingled waters and the splitting of Tiamat, Inanna's descent, the flood, and Gilgamesh's argument with death.

profile.cosmicNature: Ordered out of a murdered body, and permanently precarious. The world is built from the corpse of Tiamat, split like a shellfish to make sky and earth, and the order imposed on her is an achievement rather than a given. There is no cycle of ages and no promised end: the universe simply continues, held in place by the gods and by the rites people owe them, and the fear running under the literature is not damnation but the withdrawal of that arrangement - drought, flood, plague, the enemy at the wall.
profile.natureOfDivinity: A council, and later a court. The gods are a fractious assembly who argue, vote, get drunk, and can be outmanoeuvred; authority is conferred by that assembly rather than held absolutely. Each god also owns a city, physically resident in its temple, and the fortunes of god and city rise together - which is why the pantheon is repeatedly reorganised as power moves from Nippur to Ur to Babylon to Nineveh. Divinity is bureaucratic: everything is allotted, recorded, and governed by the me, the fixed decrees of how things are to be done.
profile.afterlife: Uniformly bleak and not earned. Everyone descends to the same dust-house below - kur, the land of no return - where the dead eat clay and are clothed like birds in feathers. Rank persists a little and the offerings of living descendants ease things slightly, but there is no reward for virtue and no punishment for vice, only the fact of being dead. Gilgamesh is a two-thousand-line argument with this and loses it.
profile.systemMechanism: Humanity was made to work. In Atrahasis the lesser gods go on strike over the labour of digging the canals, and people are made from clay and the blood of a slaughtered god specifically to take the shovel from them. Human beings exist to feed the gods through sacrifice and maintain their houses; the relationship is contractual, and the flood comes because people multiplied and made too much noise for the gods to sleep, not because they sinned.
profile.canonTexts: The Enuma Elish, Babylon's creation poem; the Epic of Gilgamesh in its Old Babylonian and Standard Babylonian recensions; Atrahasis; the Descent of Inanna and its Akkadian counterpart; Ninurta's battles in Lugal-e and Anzu; and the Sumerian temple hymns, disputations and city laments.

hierarchy.title: The Mingled Waters
hierarchy.blurb: Before anything was named there were two waters, fresh and salt, mingling. Everything else is descended from them, and the world itself is built out of one of their bodies.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: The gods born inside them make noise, and the first quarrel is about sleep

hierarchy.title: The First Generations
hierarchy.blurb: A chain of paired names climbing toward the gods who matter: silt, then the totality of sky and the totality of earth, then the sky itself.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Authority arrives with An, and is immediately delegated to those who will use it

hierarchy.title: The Great Gods
hierarchy.blurb: Sky, wind and water: the one who grants authority, the one who exercises it, and the one who finds a way round it. Between them they run the world and repeatedly fail to manage each other.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Each god owns a city, and the pantheon is reorganised whenever power moves

hierarchy.title: The Lights and the Star
hierarchy.blurb: The moon fathers the sun and the morning star. Between them they measure the month, judge by day, and provide the tradition with its most written-about deity.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Inanna goes down alive to the one kingdom none of them governs

hierarchy.title: The Land of No Return
hierarchy.blurb: A dust-house below where everyone goes and no one is judged. It is administered rather than ruled: a queen who cannot leave, a vizier who serves the writ, a doorman, and a scribe who writes it all down.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Babylon rises, and a minor city god is voted king of the universe

hierarchy.title: Babylon and Assyria
hierarchy.blurb: The champion who kills Tiamat and is given fifty names, the scribe who writes what is decreed, and the Assyrian god who took the same poem and put his own name in it.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: What the gods make, they also set monsters and demons against

hierarchy.title: Monsters, Demons and Sages
hierarchy.blurb: The eleven Tiamat bred, the thieves and guardians, the demons blamed for what killed infants - and the seven sages sent up out of the water to teach people everything they could not invent.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Below all of it, people: made to work, and arguing with death anyway

hierarchy.title: Kings and Heroes
hierarchy.blurb: Made from clay and the blood of a defeated god, to dig the canals so the gods could rest. Two of them survive the flood and refuse immortality; the rest build walls, write laws, and are remembered for it.

stories.title: Apsu Cannot Sleep
stories.summary: Before heaven and earth were named there were two waters mingling, Apsu the fresh and Tiamat the salt, and the gods were born inside them. The young gods surge about and make noise, and Apsu cannot rest. He proposes to destroy them. Tiamat refuses outright, appalled at the thought of killing what they made. Apsu takes his vizier Mummu's advice instead and prepares to act. Ea hears of it, sings a spell that puts the Deep to sleep, takes his crown, kills him, and binds Mummu on a lead. Then he builds his own house on top of the body and names it the Apsu. Every Mesopotamian temple's sacred water basin carries that name, which means the sanctuary stands on a defeated primordial being and says so.

sources.book: The Seven Tablets of Creation
Babylonian Religion and Mythology

stories.title: Tiamat Makes War
stories.summary: Goaded by her other children for having done nothing while Apsu was killed, Tiamat finally acts. She bears eleven monsters, raises Kingu above all the gods as her consort and commander, and fastens the Tablet of Destinies to his chest. Anshar sends Ea against her, and he turns back. He sends Anu, who turns back. Only then does Marduk come forward, and he names his price: that his word shall fix destinies thereafter, and that the assembly shall make him king. They test him by making a garment vanish and reappear at his command, then hail him. The bargaining is the point of the scene - the poem is careful that the kingship was given rather than seized.

sources.book: The Seven Tablets of Creation
Babylonian Religion and Mythology

stories.title: Marduk Splits the Sea
stories.summary: Marduk goes out with the four winds, a bow, a net and a flood-storm. Tiamat opens her mouth to swallow him and he drives the winds into it so she cannot close it, then shoots an arrow into her belly. He splits her like a drying fish. Half he raises as the sky, setting a bolt and a guard to keep her waters from escaping; half he lays down as the earth. Her breasts become mountains, her eyes the sources of the Tigris and Euphrates, her tail the band of the sky. He sets the stars in their stations, fixes the months, and gives the moon its phases. Then he takes the Tablet of Destinies from Kingu and seals it with his own seal. The world is not made from nothing here; it is made from a body.

sources.book: The Seven Tablets of Creation

stories.title: People Made From the Blood of the Loser
stories.summary: The gods want to be relieved of their labour. Ea proposes that one of the defeated be executed to provide the material, and the assembly names Kingu as the one who incited the war. He is bound, his arteries opened, and humanity is fashioned from his blood mixed with clay - made expressly so the gods can rest. The Atrahasis poem tells it differently and more sharply: there the lesser gods go on strike, surrounding Enlil's house with torches at night and refusing to dig the canals any longer, and people are made to take the shovel. Either way the account is the same in substance. Human beings were manufactured as a labour force, out of the remains of a rebel, and their troublesome nature is inherited from him.

sources.book: The Seven Tablets of Creation

stories.title: Enlil and Ninlil
stories.summary: Ninlil's mother warns her not to bathe in the canal. She goes anyway, Enlil sees her and takes her by force, and the assembly of gods banishes him to the underworld for it. Ninlil, pregnant with the moon, follows him down. Three times on the road he disguises himself as an underworld official and lies with her again, and three more underworld gods are conceived - substitutes, so that Nanna can be released to the sky rather than held below. Read one way it explains how the moon escapes the dark each month. Read another it is an account of a woman following the man who assaulted her. The text does not choose, and translations that turn it into a courtship are supplying something that is not there.

stories.title: Inanna Takes the Me
stories.summary: Inanna travels to Eridu to visit Enki, who receives her with butter cake and beer. Drinking with her, he becomes expansive and begins handing over the me - the fixed decrees underlying every institution of civilised life, more than a hundred of them: kingship, the priestly offices, truth, falsehood, the art of the scribe, the trades, music, sexual intercourse, the kindling and extinguishing of fire. She loads them onto her boat and leaves. Sober, he sends Isimud after her seven times, each time with sea-monsters to take them back, and each time Ninshubur beats them off. Inanna lands at Uruk with the whole apparatus of civilisation and it is unloaded to celebration. Enki, told he has failed, accepts it and makes peace.

sources.book: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature

stories.title: The Descent of Inanna
stories.summary: Inanna sets her mind on the great below and goes down, having first instructed Ninshubur to raise the alarm if she does not return in three days. At each of seven gates Neti removes one of her ornaments, and when she protests he answers each time that the decrees of the underworld are perfect and must not be questioned. She arrives naked, is turned into a corpse by the eye of death, and is hung on a hook. Ninshubur does exactly as told: Enlil refuses to help, Nanna refuses, and Enki makes two sexless beings from the dirt under his fingernail and sends them down with the food and water of life. They sympathise with Ereshkigal in her pain, are granted a gift, and ask for the corpse.

sources.book: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature

stories.title: Dumuzi is Taken
stories.summary: Inanna comes back up with the galla at her heels, required to supply a substitute. They offer to take Ninshubur, and she refuses. They offer to take two other loyal servants, and she refuses. Then she finds Dumuzi sitting on his throne in fine clothes, not mourning her at all, and fixes on him the eye of death. He appeals to Utu, who turns him into a gazelle so he can run, and he is caught anyway after a friend betrays his hiding place. His sister Geshtinanna, who had read his nightmare correctly and refused to give him up even under torture, offers to take half his sentence. So he is below for half the year and she for the other half. Women wept for Tammuz annually for two thousand years afterwards.

sources.book: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature
Semitic Mythology (Mythology of All Races V)

stories.title: Nergal and Ereshkigal
stories.summary: The gods hold a feast. Ereshkigal cannot leave the underworld and sends Namtar up to collect her portion; Nergal fails to stand when he enters, which is an insult, and is sent below to make amends. Ea coaches him: accept no chair, no bread, no beer, and above all no woman. He refuses everything and then accepts the woman, and they spend six days in bed. On the seventh he slips away. Ereshkigal weeps, then threatens to raise the dead to eat the living unless he is sent back. He returns, drags her from the throne by the hair - and then, in the fuller version, they marry and he rules beside her. It is very nearly a comedy, and then it is a story about two lonely powers finding each other.

sources.book: Semitic Mythology (Mythology of All Races V)
The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria

stories.title: Anzu Steals the Tablet of Destinies
stories.summary: Anzu is trusted with the door of Enlil's chamber, and every day watches him lay aside the Tablet of Destinies to bathe. Desire grows until he takes it and flies to the mountains. Without it the decrees fall silent and the sanctuary loses its brightness. God after god declines to go after him, because whoever holds the tablet can unmake an arrow by speaking - which Anzu does when Ninurta first shoots. Ea supplies the answer: shoot so the arrow is bound to the bird's own pinion, so that unmaking the arrow means unmaking his wing. Ninurta does it, takes back the tablet, and is honoured. In the older Sumerian art the same creature is Imdugud, a magnificent lion-headed eagle gripping two stags, and no villain at all.

sources.book: Semitic Mythology (Mythology of All Races V)
Assyrian and Babylonian Literature

stories.title: Ninurta and the Demon of the Mountains
stories.summary: Asag sits in the mountains, and where he is the water boils and the fish die in it and the land sickens. He fathers an army from the stones. Ninurta's first attack fails and he has to be rallied by his talking mace Sharur, who flies back and forth to Enlil for counsel. When Ninurta finally kills him the poem turns immediately to engineering: the waters that had been trapped in the mountains and running to waste are gathered and channelled into the Tigris, and the fields below become productive. Then he judges the stones one by one according to whether they fought for Asag - cursing flint to be shattered, blessing lapis to be honoured. A monster-killing that ends in an irrigation project and a mineralogy is a very Mesopotamian shape of story.

sources.book: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature

stories.title: Adapa Refuses the Bread of Life
stories.summary: Adapa is fishing when the south wind capsizes his boat. In his anger he curses it and breaks its wing, and for seven days the wind does not blow. Anu summons him. Ea coaches him carefully: go in mourning, flatter the two gatekeepers, and refuse the bread and water they offer you, for they are the bread and water of death. Adapa does exactly as instructed. But the gods, impressed by him and by Dumuzi and Ningishzida speaking on his behalf, offer him the bread and water of life instead - and he refuses them, as told, and so refuses immortality. Anu laughs and sends him home. Whether Ea was protecting him or keeping him mortal is a question the text does not answer.

sources.book: Semitic Mythology (Mythology of All Races V)
The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria

stories.title: The Flood
stories.summary: People multiply until their noise keeps Enlil awake, and he sends plague, then drought, then famine to reduce them. Each time Enki tells Atrahasis how to survive. When the gods resolve on a flood and bind themselves by oath to warn no one, Enki keeps the letter of his oath by speaking the warning to a reed wall, with Atrahasis behind it. He builds a boat, seals it, loads it, and rides out seven days of storm during which the gods are terrified by what they have done and Ishtar cries out that she has destroyed her own people. When it is over he releases birds to find land and makes an offering, and the starving gods gather round it like flies. Enlil is furious to find a survivor, and is talked round.

sources.book: The Epic of Gilgamish

stories.title: Enkidu is Made and Made Human
stories.summary: Gilgamesh takes what he wants in Uruk until the people complain to the gods, and Aruru washes her hands, pinches off clay and throws it into the wilderness. Enkidu is born hairy, running with the gazelles, filling in the hunters' pits. A trapper brings Shamhat to the watering place; she waits, opens her robe, and stays with him seven days. Afterwards the animals will not have him and he finds that he can think. She teaches him to wear cloth, to eat bread, to drink beer until his face brightens, and takes him to the city. The poem treats this as the making of a human being, without irony and without shame - the encounter is the mechanism of civilisation rather than a fall from grace.

sources.book: The Epic of Gilgamish

stories.title: The Killing of Humbaba
stories.summary: Gilgamesh decides to go to the Cedar Forest and kill its guardian, so as to make a name that will outlast him. Enkidu, who has seen the forest, tries to talk him out of it and comes anyway. Ninsun goes up to the roof, burns incense, complains to Shamash for having given her son a restless heart, and adopts Enkidu as her own so he will have a family. In the forest Shamash pins Humbaba with thirteen winds. Humbaba begs for his life and offers to serve, and Enkidu tells Gilgamesh to finish it. Humbaba curses them both as he dies. They cut the tallest cedar for a door and float it home. The gods will hold a council about this, and one of the two will have to die for it.

sources.book: The Epic of Gilgamish

stories.title: The Bull of Heaven
stories.summary: Ishtar proposes marriage to Gilgamesh and he refuses her, cruelly, listing her previous lovers and what became of each. She goes to Anu and demands the Bull of Heaven. He objects that it will bring seven years of famine; she threatens to break the doors of the underworld and let the dead out to eat the living, and he yields. The bull comes down and snorts, and pits open in the ground that swallow scores of men at a time. Enkidu seizes it by the tail while Gilgamesh drives a sword between the neck and the horns. Then Enkidu tears off a haunch and hurls it at Ishtar, shouting that he would do the same to her if he could. That is the second offence, and it settles which of them dies.

sources.book: The Epic of Gilgamish

stories.title: The Death of Enkidu
stories.summary: The gods decide one of the two must die, and choose Enkidu. He does not die in battle. He takes a fever and lies twelve days, and says plainly that he is afraid and that he wishes he had fallen fighting instead of like this. He curses the trapper and curses Shamhat for civilising him, until Shamash reminds him she gave him bread, friendship and a king who will mourn him, and he takes the curse back and blesses her. He dreams of the house of dust: the dead sitting in darkness, clothed like birds in feathers, eating clay, with Belet-seri kneeling before Ereshkigal reading out the register. Gilgamesh will not allow him to be buried until a maggot falls from his nose.

sources.book: The Epic of Gilgamish

stories.title: Siduri Tells Him to Go Home
stories.summary: Gilgamesh goes out into the wilderness in skins, hollow-cheeked, looking for a way not to die. At Mount Mashu the scorpion-men question him, warn him the passage is twelve leagues of darkness no one has walked, and open the gate anyway. He runs it in the dark and comes out in a garden of jewelled trees. At the tavern on the shore Siduri bolts the door against him, then lets him in, then tells him the thing everyone remembers: the life you are looking for you will not find, because when the gods made humanity they kept life for themselves. So fill your belly, be happy day and night, wash and put on clean clothes, look at the child who holds your hand, let your wife delight in you. He does not take the advice. He asks the way across instead.

sources.book: The Epic of Gilgamish

stories.title: The Snake Takes the Plant
stories.summary: Gilgamesh crosses the waters of death and finds Utnapishtim, who tells him the flood story and then sets him a test: stay awake seven nights. He fails at once, and a loaf is baked each day beside him to prove how long he slept. As a consolation he is told of a thorny plant on the seabed that makes an old man young. He ties stones to his feet, sinks, takes it, and starts home meaning to test it on an old man in Uruk first. On the way he bathes in a pool, and a snake smells the plant and carries it off, sloughing its skin as it goes. He sits down and weeps. Then he shows the ferryman the walls of Uruk, and the poem ends on the only immortality it allows: the thing you built.

sources.book: The Epic of Gilgamish

stories.title: The Curse of Agade
stories.summary: Sargon's Akkad is the wealthiest city in the world, and Inanna is its patron. Then she abandons it. Naram-Sin, denied a favourable omen for rebuilding Enlil's temple at Nippur, waits seven years, then takes an axe to the Ekur himself, tears out its doorframes and carries off its treasure. Enlil answers by bringing down the Gutians from the mountains, a people the poem describes as not classed among people, with the instincts of dogs and the features of monkeys. Famine follows, and prices are quoted in the text to make the point. Akkad is destroyed so completely that its site has never been found. Modern historians blame a severe drought around 2200 BC; the poem blames a king who lost his temper with a god.

stories.title: Etana Flies to Heaven
stories.summary: An eagle and a snake swear friendship over a tree and share their food. The eagle eats the snake's young. The snake appeals to Shamash, who tells it to hide inside a dead bull; the eagle comes down to feed, is caught, has its wings torn off and is thrown into a pit to die. Etana, king of Kish and childless, finds it there and nurses it back to health, and asks in return to be carried to heaven where the plant of birth grows. They fly, and at each league the eagle tells him to look down: the land is a hill, the sea a courtyard, then a gardener's ditch, then nothing at all. Then the tablets break. The King List names a successor, which suggests he came back with what he went for.

sources.book: Semitic Mythology (Mythology of All Races V)
Assyrian and Babylonian Literature

stories.title: The Exaltation of Inanna
stories.summary: Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon and high priestess of the moon at Ur, is driven out of her office during a rebellion and exiled. She composes a hymn appealing to Inanna, and she signs it - naming herself, describing her own suffering, and speaking about the act of composing it while she cannot sleep. She says the moon god has done nothing for her and that she turns to Inanna instead. She is restored. The hymn was copied by scribes for centuries afterwards, which is how it survives. She is generally called the earliest author known anywhere by name, though some scholars argue the texts were written later in her voice. A broken limestone disc bearing her name and image was dug up at Ur in the 1920s.

sources.book: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature
Semitic Mythology (Mythology of All Races V)

stories.title: Gudea Builds a Temple From a Dream
stories.summary: Gudea of Lagash dreams of a man as tall as the sky with a lapis tablet, a woman holding a stylus and a star map, and a donkey pawing the ground. He cannot read it, so he takes it to Nanshe, the goddess who interprets dreams, and she explains: the man is Ningirsu, the tablet is the plan of his temple, and the donkey pawing is Gudea himself impatient to build. What follows is the fullest account of a building project to survive from the ancient world - the purification of the city, cedar from the Amanus and diorite from Magan and gold from Meluhha, the making of the first brick in its mould, the seven days of feasting when the god is installed. It is written on two clay cylinders, the longest Sumerian text on any single object.

sources.book: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature
Semitic Mythology (Mythology of All Races V)

stories.title: Erra Empties Babylon
stories.summary: Erra is roused and wants slaughter. He persuades Marduk to leave his throne to have his regalia cleaned, and in the god's absence there is no order in Babylon at all. What follows is a catalogue of a city destroying itself: the citizen killed by his neighbour, the governor who gives the order, the shrine looted, the population emptied out. Ishum, his herald, argues with him throughout, and only after the damage is done does he manage to talk him to a stop and get a blessing pronounced over what is left. The poem was almost certainly written after a real catastrophe, and copies of it were hung in houses as amulets - on the reasoning that a text in which the plague god is calmed will help keep him calm.

sources.book: Semitic Mythology (Mythology of All Races V)
The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria

stories.title: Nanshe Counts What People Did
stories.summary: Once a year Nanshe reviews human conduct, and her hymn lists exactly what she is looking for. Whoever substituted a small weight for a large one. Whoever moved a boundary marker. The strong man who took from the weak. The one who said I will give and then did not give. She is described as the one who knows the orphan and knows the widow, who understands the oppression of one human being by another, and who is the orphan's mother. Alongside her stands Nisaba, goddess of grain and of the measuring reed, since honest measurement is the same subject. Ethical statements of this specificity are not common in a religion mostly concerned with correct ritual, and this hymn is among the earliest anywhere to make justice a divine concern.

entities.name: Apsu
entities.role: The freshwater abyss beneath the earth; the first being
entities.bio: The fresh water under the earth, who mingled with Tiamat before anything was named, and who was killed by his own great-grandson for wanting quiet.
entities.longBio: The Enuma Elish opens before the naming of heaven and earth, with two waters mingling their bodies: Apsu the fresh and Tiamat the salt. The gods are born inside them, and are immediately a nuisance - they surge about and make noise, and Apsu cannot sleep. He proposes to destroy them. Tiamat refuses, appalled at the idea of killing what they made, but Apsu takes the counsel of his vizier Mummu and prepares to act anyway. Ea learns of it, puts Apsu to sleep with a spell, strips off his crown and kills him, and then builds his own house on top of the dead body and names it the Apsu. That house is the temple at Eridu. A Mesopotamian sanctuary quite literally stands on a defeated primordial being, and the sacred water basin in the courtyard is named for him.
entities.variantTraditions: In Sumerian usage Abzu is more a place than a person - the freshwater deep that Enki governs, and the name of the sacred basin in a temple courtyard. The personification as a father-god who is murdered is developed in the Babylonian poem.

entities.name: Tiamat
entities.role: The salt sea; mother of the gods and of the monsters raised against them
entities.bio: The salt sea who bore the gods, refused to destroy them, and then made war on them when they killed her husband - and whose body became the world.
entities.longBio: Tiamat is the more sympathetic of the two primordials for most of the poem. When Apsu proposes to kill their noisy children she rejects it outright. Only after Ea has killed Apsu, and her other children goad her for having done nothing, does she act - and then she acts completely, bearing eleven monsters, giving Kingu the Tablet of Destinies and setting him at their head. God after god is sent against her and turns back. Marduk agrees to fight on condition that he be made king. He nets her, drives the winds into her mouth so she cannot close it, shoots an arrow into her belly and splits her like a drying fish - half raised as the sky with her waters held back by a bolt and a guard, half laid down as the earth. Her eyes become the sources of the Tigris and Euphrates. Later art shows her as a dragon; the poem does not describe her that way.
entities.variantTraditions: The familiar image of Tiamat as a great dragon is largely a modern and late reading. The Enuma Elish never gives her a clear body, and the nineteenth-century identification of her with a horned serpent on Assyrian seals is now generally rejected.

entities.name: Mummu
entities.role: Vizier of Apsu, who advised him to destroy the gods
entities.bio: Apsu's minister, who urged him to kill the young gods and was bound and stripped of his crown alongside him.
entities.longBio: Mummu appears briefly and consequentially. When Apsu complains that he cannot sleep for the noise of the gods, it is Mummu who tells him to destroy them - Tiamat has already refused - and Apsu embraces him for the advice. When Ea works his spell, he does not kill Mummu but binds him, takes his crown and holds him on a lead. The name is obscure and has been read as craftsman, as the spoken creative word, and as mist rising off water where fresh meets salt; no reading commands agreement. That so minor a figure survives at all is a reminder of how much of this literature comes down to us in fragments where a name is legible and its meaning is not.
entities.variantTraditions: The meaning of the name is genuinely unsettled. Damascius, writing in Greek nine centuries later, treats Moymis as the son of the first pair, which may preserve a real tradition or may be a Neoplatonist tidying up.

entities.name: Lahmu
entities.role: First-born of Apsu and Tiamat, with his sister-consort Lahamu
entities.bio: The first god born of the mingled waters, later demoted from creation-figure to protective doorway spirit.
entities.longBio: Lahmu and Lahamu are the first pair born when Apsu and Tiamat mingle, and from them come Anshar and Kishar. Their name has traditionally been rendered as the muddy or hairy ones, taken as the silt where the two waters meet, though the etymology is not secure. What is striking is their afterlife: by the first millennium the lahmu is no longer a cosmic ancestor but a class of protective spirit, a naked bearded hero with six curls of hair, carved at gateways and buried in figurine form under thresholds to keep out what should not come in. A being from the opening lines of the creation poem ends as a household ward, which is roughly what happened to a great deal of the older Sumerian material.
entities.variantTraditions: The plural lahmu of Assyrian gate sculpture and apotropaic figurines is probably a different development from the primordial ancestor of the Enuma Elish, sharing a name rather than an identity.

entities.name: Lahamu
entities.role: Sister-consort of Lahmu; of the first generation born from the waters
entities.bio: The female half of the first pair born from Apsu and Tiamat, named in the theogony and given almost nothing else to do.
entities.longBio: Lahamu exists in the sources as one half of a formula. The Enuma Elish names her, has her bear Anshar and Kishar with Lahmu, and moves on; she takes no part in the war and speaks no lines. She is worth including precisely for that, because the shape of a Mesopotamian theogony is a chain of paired names climbing toward the gods who actually matter, and most of the links are as thin as this one. The pattern of male-and-female pairs whose only function is to produce the next pair recurs across the ancient Near East, and turns up again in the Greek theogony by routes that are argued about but not doubted.
entities.variantTraditions: Some god-lists give a longer chain of such pairs between Lahamu and Anshar, with names that vary between copies; the Enuma Elish gives the short version.

entities.name: Anshar
entities.role: The whole of the sky; father of Anu, who sent the gods against Tiamat
entities.bio: The sky-horizon who chairs the gods' war council, sends out three champions against Tiamat, and is refused by two of them.
entities.longBio: Anshar and Kishar are born to Lahmu and Lahamu, and their names are usually taken as the totality of sky and the totality of earth - the whole of each, before either is a place. In the war narrative Anshar is the presiding elder who has to find someone willing to fight. He sends Ea, who turns back; he sends Anu, who turns back; only then does Marduk come forward, and only on terms. Anshar's function in the poem is to make the assembly's helplessness visible, so that Marduk's kingship looks earned rather than seized. In Assyria the name was pressed into service in a different way: Ashur was written with signs that let him be identified with Anshar, giving the Assyrian national god a claim to be older than Marduk.
entities.variantTraditions: The Assyrian identification of Ashur with Anshar is a theological argument conducted through spelling, and is one of the clearest cases of a pantheon being rearranged for reasons of state.

entities.name: Kishar
entities.role: The whole of the earth; consort of Anshar
entities.bio: The earth-totality paired with Anshar, mother of Anu, and like her mother little more than a name in the chain.
entities.longBio: Kishar completes the second pair of the theogony and bears Anu. As with Lahamu, the sources give her a name, a partner and a child, and no story. The pairing of Anshar and Kishar as sky-whole and earth-whole is a neat conceptual step in the poem: the primordial waters produce silt, the silt produces the totalities of sky and earth, and only then are there gods with personalities. Whether that scheme was ever a living belief or was constructed by the poem's author as a tidy genealogy is not something the evidence settles.
entities.variantTraditions: The reading of the names as totalities of sky and earth is standard but rests on etymology rather than on any text explaining them.

entities.name: Nammu
entities.role: The Sumerian primeval sea, who bore heaven and earth and made humanity
epithets: the mother who gave birth to heaven and earth
domains: the making of people from clay
entities.bio: The Sumerian first mother, older than the Babylonian scheme, who bore An and Ki and roused Enki to make humanity.
entities.longBio: Nammu belongs to the Sumerian material rather than the Enuma Elish, and gives a different and probably older account. She is the sea that existed first, and she bears An and Ki - heaven and earth - without a partner. In Enki and Ninmah she is the one who wakes her sleeping son when the lesser gods complain about their labour, telling him to make a substitute worker; Enki names the clay over the Apsu, and Nammu and the birth goddesses pinch off the pieces. Notably her name is written with the sign for the Apsu itself. That the Babylonian poem replaced this quiet, competent mother with the murdered Apsu and the defeated Tiamat is one of the sharpest examples of what the later tradition did to the earlier one.
entities.variantTraditions: Nammu largely disappears after the Old Babylonian period. Whether she was displaced by Tiamat or simply fell out of use is not clear from the record.

entities.name: Anu
entities.role: God of the sky; nominal head of the pantheon
symbols: the star sign that also means god
entities.abode: The highest heaven, above the sky of the stars
entities.bio: The sky, whose name is written with the sign that means both heaven and god, and whose authority is real but almost never exercised.
entities.longBio: Anu sits at the head of every god-list and does very little. He is the source of legitimacy: kingship descends from him, the great gods hold their offices by his grant, and the phrase anutu, Anu-ship, means sovereignty itself. But in the narratives he is remote and often ineffectual. Sent against Tiamat, he turns back without fighting. When Ishtar demands the Bull of Heaven he objects, is called a coward, and hands it over. His city Uruk kept his temple, though there Inanna increasingly took the practical role. The pattern - a sky father who is supreme in theory and passive in practice, superseded by an active storm or champion god - recurs widely enough across Indo-European and Near Eastern material to be one of the most durable observations in comparative mythology.
entities.variantTraditions: In Sumerian he is An, in Akkadian Anu. His consort is Ki in the Sumerian scheme and Antu in the Akkadian, which is simply his own name given a feminine ending.

entities.name: Ki
entities.role: The earth, consort of An, mother of Enlil
entities.bio: The earth as An's counterpart, whose separation from him by their son Enlil made the world habitable.
entities.longBio: In the Sumerian account heaven and earth are joined until they are forced apart. An carries off the sky, Enlil carries off the earth, and the space between them is where everything afterwards happens - the separation is the act that makes a world rather than a mass. Ki is rarely worshipped as a person and is often hard to distinguish from Ninhursag, who takes over her functions as the mother goddess with actual cult. In Akkadian she is replaced by Antu, a colourless figure formed from Anu's own name. The forcible parting of a sky father and an earth mother by their child is another of those patterns that recurs from Greece to Polynesia, and the Sumerian version is among the oldest written down.
entities.variantTraditions: Ki may never have had a real cult; some scholars doubt she was worshipped as a distinct goddess at all, and read her as a cosmological term that acquired a genealogy.

entities.name: Enlil
entities.role: Lord Wind; king of the gods and holder of the Tablet of Destinies
domains: the decrees that govern the world
entities.abode: The Ekur, his temple at Nippur
entities.bio: The executive power of the pantheon: the wind, the giver of kingship, and the god who decided to drown humanity because it was too loud.
entities.longBio: Enlil is the god who actually runs things. Anu grants authority; Enlil exercises it. No Sumerian king was legitimate without recognition at his temple in Nippur, and the Tablet of Destinies - possession of which is effectively the right to determine what happens - is his. He is also genuinely frightening. He is the wind in both senses: the breath that makes crops grow, and the storm that flattens the city. In Atrahasis he responds to human overpopulation and noise first with plague, then with drought, then with famine, and finally with the flood, and is furious when Enki warns a man. Yet the same god is exiled to the underworld for raping Ninlil and follows her down to make it right. He is not moral, and the literature does not pretend he is; he is powerful, and must be housed and fed.
entities.variantTraditions: Enlil's supremacy fades as Babylon rises. The Enuma Elish transfers his functions and even his epithets to Marduk, and in Assyria to Ashur, in each case by rewriting rather than by argument.

entities.name: Ninlil
entities.role: Lady Wind; consort of Enlil, mother of the moon
entities.abode: Nippur, and the underworld she followed Enlil into
entities.bio: The wind-lady who was raped by Enlil at the canal, followed him into exile underground, and bore the moon there.
entities.longBio: The Sumerian poem Enlil and Ninlil is difficult reading and is not softened here. Her mother warns her not to bathe in the canal; she does, Enlil sees her and takes her by force, and the assembly of gods banishes him to the underworld for it. Ninlil, pregnant with Nanna the moon, follows him down. What happens next is strange: Enlil disguises himself three times as underworld officials and lies with her again three times, and three more underworld gods are conceived, who serve as substitutes so that Nanna can be released to the sky. Read one way it is an aetiology of how the moon escapes darkness each month. Read another it is an account of a woman pursuing a man who has already assaulted her. The text does not resolve which, and translations that make it a courtship are importing something that is not there.
entities.variantTraditions: Under the name Sud she is a goddess of Shuruppak in her own right, and a separate poem, Enlil and Sud, tells a straightforward and consensual courtship and marriage. The two traditions were harmonised by declaring Sud to be renamed Ninlil at her wedding.

entities.name: Enki
entities.role: Lord of the freshwater deep; god of wisdom, craft and cunning
symbols: two streams flowing from his shoulders
entities.abode: The Apsu, his house at Eridu
entities.bio: The clever god: he makes people, keeps the arts of civilisation, and repeatedly saves humanity by finding a way around instructions he cannot openly defy.
entities.longBio: Enki's method is never force. Told by Apsu's plot, he sings him to sleep and kills him. Told by the assembly not to warn anyone of the flood, he speaks to a reed wall while Atrahasis happens to be behind it, keeping the letter of an oath he is deliberately breaking. When Inanna gets him drunk and talks him out of the me - the decrees underlying every institution of civilised life - he sends seven parties to retrieve them and fails, and accepts it. He makes humanity from clay so the lesser gods can stop digging, and then, when Ninmah drunkenly fashions seven defective people to spite him, finds a place in society for each of them. He is a patron of exorcists and of anyone whose work is done by knowing the right words. Where Enlil is authority, Enki is competence, and the literature clearly prefers his company.
entities.variantTraditions: Enki is the Sumerian name, Ea the Akkadian; the two are the same god throughout. The old derivation of Ea from a Sumerian phrase meaning house of water is now generally abandoned.

entities.name: Ninhursag
entities.role: Lady of the Mountain; the mother goddess who shapes life from clay
entities.bio: The mother goddess who pinches humanity out of clay, and who once cursed Enki nearly to death and then relented.
entities.longBio: Ninhursag carries so many names - Ninmah, Nintu, Aruru, Damgalnuna - that scholars still argue over how many originally distinct goddesses were merged into her. Her core function is constant: she makes bodies. She assists at the making of humanity from clay, she is invoked at childbirth, and it is she who forms Enkidu out of pinched clay to be Gilgamesh's match. The strangest story attached to her is Enki and Ninhursag, in which Enki eats the eight plants she has grown and she curses him with the eye of death, so that eight parts of his body begin to fail; she is coaxed back, seats him in her vulva, and gives birth to eight healing deities, one per afflicted part. It reads as an incantation given narrative form, and it contains the pun that produced the goddess Ninti, whose name means both lady of the rib and lady of life.
entities.variantTraditions: The Ninti pun has been argued since the 1940s to lie behind Eve being made from Adam's rib, the Hebrew account keeping the rib and dropping the wordplay that made it make sense. The connection is plausible and much repeated, but it is not proven.

entities.name: Nanna
entities.role: The moon; father of the sun and of Inanna
entities.bio: The moon god of Ur, conceived in the underworld, who crosses the night sky in a boat and whose phases gave the calendar its shape.
entities.longBio: Nanna is the son Ninlil bore underground, released to the sky by the substitution of three other children. He crosses the night in a crescent boat, and because the Mesopotamian month began with the first sighting of the new crescent, he is the god by whom time is actually reckoned - which makes him, alongside Utu, a judge, since the calendar governs when obligations fall due. His city Ur was the seat of an empire, and the office of his high priestess was held by royal daughters, among them Enheduanna, the earliest author anywhere whose name is attached to surviving work. His other great sanctuary at Harran outlived Babylon by a very long way: moon worship persisted there into the Islamic period, centuries after cuneiform had been forgotten.
entities.variantTraditions: Sumerian Nanna and Akkadian Sin are the same god. The bull's horns and the crescent are deliberately conflated in the imagery, and cattle-herding metaphors run all through his hymns.

entities.name: Ningal
entities.role: Great Lady; consort of the moon, mother of the sun and of Inanna
entities.bio: The moon's consort, mother of Utu and Inanna, and the voice of the great lament for the destruction of her city.
entities.longBio: Ningal is the daughter of Ningikuga and Enki, and marries Nanna at Ur, where the two of them are the city's divine household. Her most powerful appearance is in the Lament for Ur, composed after the Elamites sacked the city around 2000 BC. In it she describes pleading with An and Enlil not to destroy Ur, being refused, and having to watch: the corpses in the gates, the dead lying like fat in the sun, the temple standing empty. The city laments are among the most affecting things in the whole corpus, and they are theologically hard - the god of the city cannot save it, because the destruction was decreed by the higher gods, and all she can do is grieve. Her name travelled west as Nikkal and is still met in Ugaritic and later Aramaic contexts.
entities.variantTraditions: As Nikkal she appears in Ugaritic myth, married to the moon god Yarikh, and the name survives into Syriac and Arabic usage.

entities.name: Utu
entities.role: The sun; judge of gods and men
symbols: the solar disc with four points and rays
entities.bio: The sun who sees everything that happens by day, and is therefore the god before whom oaths are sworn and cases are judged.
entities.longBio: Utu rises through the eastern gates each morning, crosses the sky, and enters the west, passing through the underworld at night where he brings light and judgement to the dead as well. Because nothing done in daylight escapes him, he became the god of justice in the plainest sense: contracts were sworn before him, disputes settled in his name, and the stele of Hammurabi's laws shows the king receiving the rod and ring from him. He carries a saw, used in the iconography to cut through the mountains at dawn and, by extension, to cut through legal cases. He is a reliably helpful god in the narratives - he answers Gilgamesh, protects Dumuzi when the demons come for him, and stands behind travellers on the road. Among a pantheon of dangerous personalities he is one of very few who can simply be trusted.
entities.variantTraditions: Utu is the Sumerian name and Shamash the Akkadian, the latter cognate with the ordinary Semitic word for sun. The gender is fixed as male here, unlike the Anatolian and Germanic sun deities.

entities.name: Aya
entities.role: The dawn; bride of the sun
entities.bio: The dawn goddess who wakes the sun, and who is petitioned to speak to him on the worshipper's behalf.
entities.longBio: Aya - Sherida in Sumerian - is the sun's wife and the light before he appears. Her cult ran alongside Shamash's at Sippar for the whole of Mesopotamian history, and her role in prayer is specific and revealing: worshippers ask her to intercede, to speak a good word to her husband about them. That pattern of approaching a powerful god through a sympathetic consort is one of the ordinary mechanics of Mesopotamian religion, and it tells you something about how people expected divine and royal households alike to work. She is also invoked in connection with sexual love and with the marriage bed, and her epithet kallatu, the bride, is used so consistently that it functions as a second name.
entities.variantTraditions: The Sumerian Sherida is attested from very early on at Sippar; Aya is the Akkadian name for the same goddess, and the two are used interchangeably in bilingual texts.

entities.name: Inanna
entities.role: Queen of Heaven; goddess of sexual love and of war
entities.bio: The most written-about deity in the corpus: love and war in one person, who went down to the underworld alive and came back by sending her husband in her place.
entities.longBio: Inanna is not a fertility goddess in the placid sense that phrase suggests. She is desire and she is battle, and the hymns describe her delighting in both; a proverb has it that she can turn a man into a woman and a woman into a man, and her cult included personnel whose gender did not fit ordinary categories. She has no stable consort and no children to speak of - her power is her own rather than derived from a husband, unusually among the great goddesses. Her defining narrative is the descent: she goes down to her sister Ereshkigal's kingdom for reasons the text never quite explains, is stripped at each of seven gates, is judged, killed and hung on a hook, is revived by Enki's cunning, and is released only on condition she provide a substitute. She chooses Dumuzi, because he did not mourn her. As Venus she is both morning and evening star, which is presumably why she is so consistently double.
entities.variantTraditions: Sumerian Inanna and Akkadian Ishtar were originally distinct and were merged early. Her descent survives in both a Sumerian and a shorter Akkadian version, differing in detail; the Akkadian text says the world's sexual activity ceased while she was below, which the Sumerian does not.

entities.name: Dumuzi
entities.role: The shepherd; Inanna's husband, given to the underworld in her place
entities.bio: The shepherd husband who was seized by demons as Inanna's substitute, and who spends half of each year below and half above.
entities.longBio: Dumuzi wins Inanna in a courtship poem where he competes with Enkimdu the farmer, and the love songs between them are frankly erotic and among the oldest surviving anywhere. The story turns when Inanna returns from the dead with the galla demons at her heels, required to hand over a replacement. She finds Dumuzi sitting on his throne in fine clothes, not mourning her, and fixes on him the eye of death. He runs, Utu turns him into a gazelle to help him escape, and he is caught anyway. His sister Geshtinanna volunteers to take half his sentence, so he is below for half the year and she for the other half. Women wept for Tammuz annually in a rite that spread across the Near East, and is complained about by name in the book of Ezekiel, where the prophet is shown women weeping for him at the north gate of the temple in Jerusalem.
entities.variantTraditions: The old scholarly category of the dying-and-rising god, built partly on Dumuzi, has been heavily criticised; his alternation with his sister is a shared sentence rather than a resurrection, and the sources never describe him as conquering death.

entities.name: Geshtinanna
entities.role: Dumuzi's sister, who took half his term in the underworld; interpreter of dreams
epithets: the divine scribe of the underworld
entities.abode: The steppe, and the underworld for half the year
entities.bio: The sister who refused to give her brother up, and took half his sentence among the dead so he could have half a year in the light.
entities.longBio: Geshtinanna is one of the few figures in this literature who acts out of plain loyalty and gains nothing by it. Dumuzi comes to her with a nightmare, and she reads it for him correctly: the reeds rising against him, the churn falling silent, all of it means he is going to be taken. She hides him. When the demons come she refuses to say where he is even under torture, and it is a friend who betrays him instead. Afterwards she volunteers to spend half of each year below in his place. She also has an office in her own right as the scribe of the underworld, the one who keeps the record of the dead, and as a reader of dreams - which fits, since the dream she reads is the one that structures the whole story.
entities.variantTraditions: Her name means vine of heaven, and she is associated with the autumn wine while Dumuzi is associated with the spring; their alternation has often been read as a seasonal scheme, though the texts do not spell one out.

entities.name: Ninshubur
entities.role: Inanna's vizier and messenger, who went to the gods to get her back
entities.bio: The servant who did exactly as instructed and saved her mistress, and who is the reason the descent does not simply end with a corpse on a hook.
entities.longBio: Before going down, Inanna gives Ninshubur precise orders: if I do not return in three days, mourn for me, then go to Enlil, then to Nanna, then to Enki, and beg each of them to save me. Ninshubur does all of it. Enlil refuses, Nanna refuses, and Enki - who is always the one who finds a way - fashions two sexless beings from the dirt under his fingernail, gives them the food and water of life, and sends them down. Ninshubur is later offered to the demons as a substitute and Inanna refuses to give her up, which is the one moment of decency in the goddess's treatment of anybody. In Akkadian usage the role is taken over by Papsukkal, and the gender of the figure shifts between traditions.
entities.variantTraditions: Ninshubur is female in most Sumerian sources and merges in Akkadian with the male Papsukkal; the sources are not consistent, and the figure is better understood as an office than a fixed person.

entities.name: Ereshkigal
entities.role: Queen of the Great Below; Inanna's sister
epithets: queen of the land of no return
symbols: the lapis measuring rod and line
the throne of the great below
entities.abode: Irkalla, the land of no return
entities.bio: The queen of the dead, who is not evil and is not free: she rules the underworld and can never leave it.
entities.longBio: Ereshkigal governs kur, the land from which there is no coming back, and the rules there are not hers to bend - they are the ancient decrees, and she is bound by them as much as anyone. When Inanna arrives demanding entry she is furious and frightened, and the seven gates that strip her sister are the law rather than spite. What is most striking about her is how unhappy she is. In the Descent she is described writhing like a woman in labour with nothing to give birth to, and in Nergal and Ereshkigal she weeps at being confined below and denied the pleasures of the upper gods. She is not a devil; there is no devil in this system. She is an administrator of something nobody wants, in a place she cannot leave, and the literature grants her that dignity.
entities.variantTraditions: The Akkadian version of the descent has Ishtar threaten to break the door and let the dead out to eat the living, a line with no Sumerian counterpart and a long afterlife in later apocalyptic imagery.

entities.name: Nergal
entities.role: God of plague and of the scorching sun; king of the underworld beside Ereshkigal
entities.bio: The god of plague and burning heat who came down to the underworld to apologise, and stayed as its king.
entities.longBio: Nergal is the sun at its worst - the heat that kills crops and brings fever - and by extension war and epidemic. His route to the throne of the dead is told in Nergal and Ereshkigal, which is very nearly a comedy until it is not. The gods hold a feast; Ereshkigal cannot attend and sends her vizier Namtar to collect her portion; Nergal fails to stand when Namtar enters, an insult, and is sent down to make amends. Warned by Ea not to accept the chair, the bread, the beer or the woman, he refuses everything and then accepts the woman, and they spend six days in bed. He slips away; she threatens to raise the dead to eat the living unless he is returned; he comes back, drags her from the throne by the hair - and then, in the fuller version, they marry, and he rules beside her. His other great poem, Erra and Ishum, has him depopulate Babylon for the pleasure of it and then be talked down.
entities.variantTraditions: Nergal and the plague god Erra are treated as one god here, following most of the later material, though they were probably distinct in origin.

entities.name: Namtar
entities.role: Fate; vizier of the underworld and bringer of disease
entities.bio: Death as an appointed official: the fate that is cut for you, personified as Ereshkigal's minister and the carrier of sixty diseases.
entities.longBio: The name means something like the cut, the thing decreed and separated off, and Namtar is fate in its narrowest sense - not destiny in general but the specific sentence that ends a particular life. He carries out Ereshkigal's orders, and it is he who strikes Inanna with sixty diseases when she is judged. Incantations against illness address him directly and try to send him back, and he is one of the figures most often named in medical texts, since a disease and its demon were not clearly separate things. His parentage is given as Enlil and Ereshkigal in some sources, which makes him a bureaucrat of impeccable family. Like Ereshkigal he is not evil; he is the officer who serves the writ.
entities.variantTraditions: Namtar sits on the boundary between god and demon, a distinction Mesopotamian sources draw much less sharply than later traditions do.

entities.name: Neti
entities.role: The chief gatekeeper of the underworld
domains: the enforcement of the rules of the dead
entities.bio: The doorman who takes Inanna's orders to the queen and then strips her of one ornament at each of the seven gates.
entities.longBio: Neti's role is small, procedural and central. Inanna arrives above and pounds on the gate; Neti asks who she is and what she wants, goes to Ereshkigal for instructions, and returns to carry them out. At each of the seven gates he removes one item - the crown, the rod and line, the necklace, the breast ornaments, the girdle, the bangles, the robe - and when Inanna protests each time, his answer is the same: be silent, the decrees of the underworld are perfect, do not question the rites. That refrain is the theological centre of the poem. The underworld is not cruel and is not negotiable, and the goddess of everything arrives at the throne naked and bowed low, like everyone else.
entities.variantTraditions: The seven gates and the stripping have no obvious parallel elsewhere in the corpus and may be specific to this composition; the number seven is standard for completeness in Mesopotamian ritual.

entities.name: Ningishzida
entities.role: Lord of the Good Tree; throne-bearer of the underworld, and a serpent god
domains: guardianship of the gate of heaven
entities.bio: A serpent god of the underworld and the roots of trees, who also stands as a doorkeeper of heaven and appears as a patron on royal seals.
entities.longBio: Ningishzida is one of the more visually memorable figures in the corpus, shown as a horned serpent or with serpent heads rising from his shoulders, and his emblem of two entwined snakes is old enough and widespread enough that it is frequently, and speculatively, connected to later caduceus imagery. He belongs below, as throne-bearer to the queen of the dead, but in Adapa's story he and Dumuzi stand at the gate of heaven, and the two of them are so moved by Adapa's account that they speak for him. Gudea of Lagash names him as his personal god on the great inscribed cylinders. He is a good illustration of how little these gods respect a tidy division between chthonic and celestial roles: the same figure guards the door of the sky and carries the throne of the dead.
entities.variantTraditions: The link between his entwined serpents and the Greek caduceus is often asserted and never demonstrated; the motif is old and widely distributed, and shared iconography is not proof of transmission.

entities.name: Belet-seri
entities.role: Lady of the Steppe; scribe who records the dead
entities.bio: The clerk of the underworld, kneeling before the queen and reading aloud from the tablet of who has arrived.
entities.longBio: Enkidu's dream of the house of dust, one of the bleakest passages in the Gilgamesh epic, ends with Belet-seri. He sees the dead sitting in darkness, clothed like birds in feathers, eating clay - and there, kneeling before Ereshkigal, is the scribe of the underworld with her tablet, reading out the record. It is a small detail that does a great deal: the underworld is not chaos but an office, everything is written down, and the writing is what makes it final. She is the Akkadian counterpart of Geshtinanna in this function, and the two are identified with each other in god-lists. The Mesopotamian afterlife is administered, and Belet-seri is the administration.
entities.variantTraditions: God-lists equate her with Geshtinanna, and her title lady of the steppe connects her to Dumuzi's territory; whether these are one goddess or two brought together is unclear.

entities.name: Marduk
entities.role: Champion of the gods and king of the pantheon; god of Babylon
entities.bio: A minor city god promoted to king of the universe when his city became an empire, who killed Tiamat and built the world from her body.
entities.longBio: Marduk is the clearest case in any mythology of a god rising with his city. In the early Sumerian record he is a local deity of Babylon of no great importance. When Babylon became the political centre under Hammurabi and again under Nebuchadnezzar, the Enuma Elish was composed to explain why the gods themselves had made him king - and it is careful to say the assembly gave him the office rather than that he took it. He alone will face Tiamat, on the condition that his word thereafter fixes destinies. He nets her, splits her, arranges the sky, sets the stars in their stations, fixes the calendar, and creates humanity from the blood of Kingu so the gods can rest. The poem closes by reciting his fifty names, absorbing the functions of fifty other gods into one. It was recited annually at the New Year festival, with the king taking part - theology and statecraft in the same ceremony.
entities.variantTraditions: Assyrian copies of the same poem replace Marduk with Ashur throughout. The two versions are otherwise nearly identical, which makes the political function of the text impossible to miss.

entities.name: Sarpanit
entities.role: Consort of Marduk; the shining one of Babylon
entities.bio: Marduk's wife, whose sacred marriage to him was enacted at the New Year and who was petitioned in pregnancy.
entities.longBio: Sarpanit is honoured chiefly as the queen of Babylon's divine household. Her name has been read as the silvery or shining one and also as she of Zarpan, a place near Babylon; neither is settled. Her most public role came at the akitu, the New Year festival, when the image of Nabu was brought from Borsippa, the destinies were fixed, and a sacred marriage between Marduk and Sarpanit was celebrated - the union on which the coming year's fertility and the king's legitimacy were both understood to rest. Privately she was invoked by women in pregnancy and childbirth, which is the ordinary religion underneath the state ceremony, and the pattern of a great goddess who is imperial in public and domestic in private is a common one.
entities.variantTraditions: She is sometimes identified with Erua and, in later syncretism, drawn together with Ishtar; the god-lists do not treat them as the same goddess.

entities.name: Nabu
entities.role: God of writing, wisdom and the scribal art; son of Marduk
epithets: keeper of the tablet of destinies
entities.bio: The scribe of the gods, who writes down what is decreed - and whose name survives in Nebuchadnezzar and in the prophet Nebo.
entities.longBio: Nabu holds the office that matters most in a civilisation built on records: he writes. The Tablet of Destinies passes into his keeping, and what he inscribes on it is what happens. As patron of scribes he was enormously popular, and by the later periods his cult rivalled his father's - the great Assyrian library at Nineveh was dedicated to him, and the standard scribal colophon asks his blessing. At the New Year his statue travelled by boat from Borsippa to Babylon to take part in the fixing of destinies, one of the great processions of the ancient world. His name is the ordinary Semitic root for announcing or prophesying, the same root behind the Hebrew nabi, prophet, and it is embedded in royal names from Nabopolassar to Nebuchadnezzar; the Hebrew Bible names him directly as Nebo, bowing down alongside Bel.
entities.variantTraditions: The relationship between Nabu and Marduk shifts over time: he is first Marduk's minister and only later his son, a promotion that follows the growth of his own cult.

entities.name: Tashmetu
entities.role: Lady of listening; consort of Nabu
entities.bio: The goddess whose name means the hearing: petitions were addressed to her because she was expected to listen and pass them on.
entities.longBio: Tashmetu's name comes from the verb to hear or to grant, and that is precisely her function. Worshippers asked her to hear them and to speak to Nabu, exactly as they asked Aya to speak to Shamash - the household model of approaching power through a sympathetic member of the family. She and Nabu are the subject of some remarkable love poetry from the Assyrian period, in which the two speak to each other in the bedchamber in language that is tender and quite unguarded, and which was probably performed as part of a festival of their marriage. Alongside the state theology of destinies and empires, this literature preserves gods who are also a couple.
entities.variantTraditions: The Nabu and Tashmetu love dialogues survive in Assyrian copies; how far they reflect Babylonian practice at Borsippa is unclear.

entities.name: Ashur
entities.role: National god of Assyria; the city, the state and the god under one name
epithets: king of the gods in Assyria
symbols: the winged disc with an archer
entities.abode: The city of Ashur, and later Nineveh
entities.bio: The god who was the city he lived in, promoted to king of the universe by rewriting Babylon's poem with his name in it.
entities.longBio: Ashur begins as something unusual: not a god who owns a city but a god who is the city, the deified site itself, without an origin story or a family. As Assyria became the dominant power, that blankness turned out to be useful - there was nothing to contradict, so material could simply be attached. Assyrian scribes copied the Enuma Elish and substituted Ashur for Marduk throughout, and spelled his name with signs that identified him with Anshar, making him older than the Babylonian champion rather than a rival to him. He was given Ninlil as a wife by reassignment. His emblem, a winged disc with an archer drawing a bow, flew over the armies that took Israel, Babylon and Egypt. When Nineveh fell in 612 BC the god fell with it, and unlike Marduk he did not outlive his state.
entities.variantTraditions: The identification with Anshar is a scribal argument rather than an old tradition, and modern scholarship treats it as deliberate theological engineering.

entities.name: Ninurta
entities.role: God of war and of the plough; the champion who kills the mountain demon
entities.bio: Enlil's warrior son, who kills the demon Asag, recovers the stolen Tablet of Destinies, and then dictates a farming manual.
entities.longBio: Ninurta is the divine champion before Marduk, and much of Marduk's material is modelled on his. In Lugal-e he goes up against Asag, a demon of the mountains whose presence makes water undrinkable and whose stone armies fight for him; Ninurta defeats him, and then dams the mountains to redirect the waters into the Tigris, turning a monster-killing into an irrigation project. He judges the stones afterwards, cursing those that fought him and blessing those that did not - an aetiology of why some minerals are precious. In the Anzu poem he recovers the Tablet of Destinies from the thunderbird that stole it. And the Farmer's Instructions, a genuine agricultural text, is framed as his advice. War god and plough god at once is not a contradiction here: both are the same seasonal violence of flood water, which either destroys the field or makes it.
entities.variantTraditions: Ningirsu, the god of Girsu honoured on Gudea's cylinders, is either the same god under a local name or a distinct god merged with him very early; the sources treat them as one from the Old Babylonian period on.

entities.name: Gula
entities.role: The great physician; goddess of healing, with her dog
epithets: the physician of the black-headed people
entities.bio: The healing goddess whose emblem is a dog, and who could impose the disease as readily as lift it.
entities.longBio: Gula is the doctor of the pantheon and one of the more frequently invoked goddesses in daily practice, addressed in medical incantations, in prayers for the sick and in the curse formulae at the end of legal documents - where she is asked to put an incurable sickness into the body of whoever breaks the contract. That double edge is the point: the power to heal is the power to withhold healing. Her animal is the dog, and dog figurines were buried at her temples and under thresholds as protection; the excavations at Isin turned up a dog cemetery attached to her sanctuary. Whether the association comes from dogs licking wounds, from their role guarding houses, or from something else, the sources do not explain, but it is consistent for two thousand years.
entities.variantTraditions: Gula, Ninisina of Isin, Nintinugga of Nippur and Bau of Lagash are separate healing goddesses who were increasingly treated as one; god-lists both equate and distinguish them depending on period.

entities.name: Adad
entities.role: The storm: rain that feeds the crop and the flood that takes it
entities.bio: The storm god, whose rain is the whole difference between harvest and famine and whose flood is the same water arriving wrong.
entities.longBio: In a land farmed by irrigation, the storm is not simply weather. Adad brings the rain that fills the canals and the hail that flattens the barley, and his hymns hold both without embarrassment: he is called lord of abundance and, a few lines later, described flattening the land like a mat. He rides or stands on a bull, holds the lightning as a forked bundle, and his bellow is thunder. In the Gilgamesh flood account it is Adad's roar that begins it. He is also, with Shamash, one of the two gods of divination, addressed in the queries that Assyrian kings put to their diviners before any campaign. West of Mesopotamia the same god is Hadad, and under that name and its variants he becomes one of the major deities of Syria and the Levant, met in the Bible as Baal-Hadad.
entities.variantTraditions: Sumerian Ishkur was a relatively minor figure; the god's importance grows sharply with Semitic-speaking populations, for whom Hadad was central.

entities.name: Shala
entities.role: Consort of the storm god; the grain-ear goddess
epithets: she of the ear of grain
entities.bio: The storm god's wife, shown holding an ear of grain - the crop that his rain either makes or destroys.
entities.longBio: Shala stands beside Adad in the iconography holding a stalk of barley, which states the relationship between them more economically than any text: he is the rain, she is what the rain produces. Her name has been connected to a word for compassion, though the etymology is uncertain and may be Hurrian rather than Semitic, since a goddess Shala is worshipped among the Hurrians as well and the direction of borrowing is unclear. A constellation was named for her - the Furrow, holding the ear of grain - and it is the same stretch of sky the Greeks later called Virgo, still shown holding a sheaf. That is one of the more durable inheritances in the whole record: the image outlived the language, the empire and the religion.
entities.variantTraditions: The identification of Shala's Furrow with the later Virgo is secure enough to be standard in histories of astronomy, and is among the clearest transmissions from Babylonian to Greek celestial tradition.

entities.name: Nisaba
entities.role: Goddess of grain and of writing; patroness of scribes before Nabu
symbols: the tablet with the star map
entities.bio: Grain and writing in one goddess, because writing began as the counting of grain.
entities.longBio: Nisaba is the most quietly revealing deity in the pantheon. She is a goddess of barley and also the goddess of the scribal art, and the reason is historical rather than symbolic: cuneiform began as accountancy, the recording of quantities of grain in and out of temple stores, and the same woman who governs the crop governs the tablet that counts it. Sumerian literary compositions routinely end with the line praise to Nisaba, which functions as a scribe's signature. She is shown with a tablet of the heavens on her knees, marking her as the one who knows the measurements of the sky as well as of the field. Her displacement by Nabu in the later periods is one of a number of cases where a prominent Sumerian goddess is replaced by an Akkadian god in the same office.
entities.variantTraditions: The alternative reading Nidaba appears in older scholarship; Nisaba is now standard.

entities.name: Nanshe
entities.role: Goddess of dreams, fish and social justice
epithets: she who cares for the widow
entities.bio: A marsh goddess who reads dreams and audits the conduct of the powerful, keeping a specific list of who mistreated whom.
entities.longBio: Nanshe is worth including for one hymn in particular. Alongside her roles interpreting dreams and governing the fish and birds of the southern marshes, she conducts a yearly review of human behaviour, and the text lists exactly what she is looking for: whoever substituted a small weight for a large one, whoever moved a boundary marker, the strong man who took from the weak, the one who said I would give but did not give. She is described as the one who knows the orphan and knows the widow. Ethical claims of that specificity are not common in Mesopotamian religion, which is generally more concerned with correct ritual than with conduct, and this hymn is often cited as one of the earliest statements anywhere of social justice as a divine concern.
entities.variantTraditions: The Nanshe Hymn survives in Old Babylonian copies of an older composition; its ethical passages have sometimes been overinterpreted as a general Mesopotamian creed, which they are not.

entities.name: Ninkasi
entities.role: Goddess of beer, born of sparkling fresh water
epithets: the lady who fills the mouth
she who was born of flowing water
entities.bio: The brewer of the gods, whose hymn is simultaneously a work of praise and a working recipe for beer.
entities.longBio: The Hymn to Ninkasi is one of the most quoted Sumerian texts for a good reason: it is a poem in her honour that also sets out, step by step, how beer was actually made - the bappir loaf twice-baked, the malt spread on mats, the mash, the filtering vat that makes a pleasant sound. Modern brewers have worked from it. Beer in Mesopotamia was a daily staple rather than a luxury, drunk through a straw from a communal jar to avoid the sediment, issued as rations, and central enough that the tavern-keeper appears in Hammurabi's laws. Ninkasi is described as born of sparkling water, and her role is entirely benign - a rarity here, since almost every other deity of consumption comes with a warning attached.
entities.variantTraditions: That the hymn preserves a genuine brewing procedure is widely accepted; how literally each stage should be read is debated among historians of food.

entities.name: Nusku
entities.role: Light and fire; vizier of Enlil
entities.bio: The lamp that burns through the night: Enlil's minister, the carrier of messages, and the fire that takes an offering upward.
entities.longBio: Nusku is fire in its useful and domestic form rather than its destructive one - the lamp lit against the dark, the flame that consumes an offering and so delivers it. As Enlil's vizier he carries messages and announces decisions, and in the Atrahasis poem it is Nusku whom Enlil sends out at night to find out why the lesser gods have surrounded his house with torches, which turns out to be a strike over their working conditions. He is invoked constantly in the anti-witchcraft rituals: the burning of a figurine of the sorcerer is addressed to him, since fire is what destroys the binding. A god of the lamp in a world without street lighting is not a small god, and his prayers are among the more personal in the corpus, spoken by people alone at night.
entities.variantTraditions: Nusku is sometimes identified with the Sumerian Gibil, another fire god; the two are distinguished in some lists and merged in others.

entities.name: Isimud
entities.role: Two-faced vizier of Enki, who looks forward and back at once
domains: the carrying out of Enki's instructions
entities.bio: Enki's messenger, shown with a face on each side of his head, who does what he is told even when he can see it is going wrong.
entities.longBio: Isimud is instantly recognisable in the art: a single head with two bearded faces looking in opposite directions, which presumably signals that a messenger must see where he came from and where he is going. His best scene is in Inanna and Enki. Enki, drunk, has given Inanna the me - the whole apparatus of civilisation - and when he sobers up he sends Isimud after her boat to get them back. Isimud catches her seven times and each time delivers the demand politely; Inanna refuses each time and her minister Ninshubur beats off the sea-monsters sent with him. He fails, and reports the failure. He also appears carrying out the arrangements in Enki and Ninhursag, ferrying messages between the two. He is a functionary rendered with real character.
entities.variantTraditions: Usmu is the Akkadian form of the name. The two-faced iconography is well attested on cylinder seals and is one of the few cases where a minor god is securely identifiable in the art.

entities.name: Enkimdu
entities.role: The farmer god, who lost Inanna to the shepherd and kept his temper
epithets: lord of the dyke and canal
entities.bio: Dumuzi's rival for Inanna, who is refused, offers the winner the run of his fields anyway, and is the only figure in the story to behave well.
entities.longBio: The Sumerians were fond of disputation poems in which two occupations argue their merits - summer and winter, the hoe and the plough, silver and copper - and Dumuzi and Enkimdu is the courtship version. The shepherd and the farmer each set out what they can give Inanna. Her brother Utu urges the shepherd; Inanna at first prefers the farmer; Dumuzi presses his case at length. When it is settled, Dumuzi comes looking for a quarrel and Enkimdu simply declines to have one, offering to let his flocks graze anywhere on his land and to bring gifts to the wedding. It is a small thing, but in a literature full of gods who kill each other over precedence, the farmer who shrugs is memorable, and the text seems to know it.
entities.variantTraditions: The poem is one of several Sumerian disputations; whether it reflects a real cultic rivalry between herding and farming interests, or is simply a literary form, is debated.

entities.name: Kingu
entities.role: Tiamat's champion and second husband; the god whose blood became humanity
epithets: holder of the Tablet of Destinies
symbols: the Tablet of Destinies on his breast
entities.abode: At the head of Tiamat's host
entities.bio: Tiamat's general, given the Tablet of Destinies and defeated with her - then executed so that people could be made from his blood.
entities.longBio: Kingu is elevated by Tiamat above all the other gods she has borne, made her consort, and given the Tablet of Destinies fastened to his chest, which is meant to make his word binding. It does not survive contact with Marduk, who takes the tablet off him and seals it with his own seal. What happens afterwards is the important part.
