When the gods want servants so they can rest, Ea proposes that one of the defeated be killed to provide the material, and the assembly names Kingu as the instigator. He is bound, his arteries are cut, and humanity is fashioned from his blood mixed with clay. People therefore carry in them the blood of the rebel who lost - which is offered as the explanation for why human beings are troublesome, mortal, and obliged to work.
entities.variantTraditions: Atrahasis names a different slaughtered god, We-ila or Geshtu-e, whose intelligence as well as blood goes into the clay. The two accounts are separate traditions rather than versions of one.

entities.name: Anzu
entities.role: The lion-headed eagle who stole the Tablet of Destinies
symbols: the lion-headed eagle with spread wings
entities.abode: The mountains, and the gate of Enlil's chamber
entities.bio: A storm-bird who waited on Enlil, stole the Tablet of Destinies while he bathed, and was hunted down by Ninurta.
entities.longBio: Anzu is trusted with the door of Enlil's private chamber, and every day he watches Enlil remove the Tablet of Destinies and set it aside to bathe. Desire grows in him until he takes it and flies to the mountains, and with it the ordered world stops: the decrees fall silent, the sanctuary loses its brightness. Several gods are asked to go after him and refuse, because whoever holds the tablet can unmake an arrow in flight by speaking - which is exactly what Anzu does when Ninurta shoots at him. Ninurta wins by taking Ea's advice: he shoots so that the arrow is bound to the bird's own pinion, so unmaking the arrow means unmaking his own wing feathers. In the older Sumerian art he is Imdugud, a lion-headed eagle shown gripping two stags, and he is a protective emblem rather than a villain.
entities.variantTraditions: The shift from Imdugud, a grand and largely benign storm-bird of Sumerian iconography, to Anzu the thief of the Akkadian poem is a real change of character and not simply a change of name.

entities.name: Asag
entities.role: The demon of the mountains, whose presence sickens the land
epithets: the one who fathered the stones
entities.bio: A demon so hideous that fish boiled alive in the rivers near him, defeated by Ninurta - who then reorganised the water supply.
entities.longBio: Asag is described in Lugal-e in terms of contamination rather than malice: where he is, water boils and fish die in it, and the land sickens. He fathers an army out of the stones of the mountain, and he is formidable enough that Ninurta's first assault fails and he has to retreat and be rallied by his talking mace Sharur. When Ninurta finally kills him, the poem does something unusual - it moves straight from the battle to hydraulics. The waters that had been held in the mountains and were running to waste are gathered and channelled into the Tigris, and the fields below become productive. Then Ninurta passes judgement on each type of stone according to whether it fought for Asag, which explains why flint shatters and lapis is honoured. A monster story that ends in an irrigation scheme and a mineralogy is a very Mesopotamian thing.
entities.variantTraditions: Asakku in Akkadian becomes a general class of disease demon rather than a single figure, invoked in medical incantations.

entities.name: Humbaba
entities.role: The guardian of the Cedar Forest, appointed by Enlil
epithets: he whose shout is the flood
symbols: a face made of coiled entrails
entities.bio: The forest's appointed guardian, killed by Gilgamesh and Enkidu for fame, and the killing is what condemns Enkidu.
entities.longBio: Humbaba was set over the Cedar Forest by Enlil to keep men out of it, and his face is described in the omen texts as looking like coiled intestines - a real observation, since the pattern of a sheep's entrails used in divination was said to resemble it. Gilgamesh goes to kill him for no better reason than to make a name that will outlast him, and Enkidu comes along despite knowing better. They win with the help of Shamash, who pins Humbaba with thirteen winds. Then he begs for his life, and offers to serve, and Enkidu tells Gilgamesh to finish it. Humbaba curses them both before he dies. The gods hold a council afterwards and decide one of the two must die for the killing of the guardian and of the Bull of Heaven, and they choose Enkidu. Read plainly, it is a story about two young men killing something that was doing its job.
entities.variantTraditions: Huwawa is the older Sumerian and Old Babylonian form; Humbaba is the later standard version. The Old Babylonian text is markedly less sympathetic to him than the later one.

entities.name: The Bull of Heaven
entities.role: The Bull of Heaven, loosed on Uruk by Ishtar in revenge
symbols: the snorting that opens pits in the earth
entities.bio: The bull Ishtar demanded from Anu after Gilgamesh insulted her, whose snorts opened pits that swallowed hundreds of men.
entities.longBio: Gilgamesh refuses Ishtar's proposal of marriage, and does it cruelly, listing her previous lovers and what became of each of them. She goes to Anu in a fury and demands the Bull of Heaven. Anu objects that it will bring seven years of famine; she threatens to smash the doors of the underworld and let the dead out to eat the living, and he gives it to her. The bull comes down and snorts, and pits open in the ground and swallow scores of young men at a time. Enkidu seizes it by the tail and Gilgamesh kills it with a sword between the neck and the horns. Then Enkidu tears off a haunch and throws it at Ishtar, shouting that he would do the same to her if he could catch her - which is the second capital offence, and it seals his death. In the sky the bull is Taurus, which the Mesopotamians already read as a bull.
entities.variantTraditions: The name Gugalanna appears in the Descent of Inanna as Ereshkigal's husband, and whether he is the same figure as the Bull of Heaven is disputed.

entities.name: Mushussu
entities.role: The horned serpent-dragon of Marduk, who paces the Ishtar Gate
symbols: scaled body with a horned head
the forelegs of a lion and the hindlegs of an eagle
entities.abode: At Marduk's feet, and on the walls of Babylon
entities.bio: The dragon that walks beside Marduk, and the single most recognisable image to survive from Babylon.
entities.longBio: The mushussu has a scaled serpent's body and neck, a horned head, a forked tongue, a lion's forelegs and an eagle's hind talons. It belonged to Tiamat's brood first, and was taken over by the victor as an attribute - which is what generally happens to defeated monsters here. It passes from Ninazu to Ningishzida to Tiamat to Marduk, following the ownership of the office rather than any family line. Its lasting fame is architectural: Nebuchadnezzar's Ishtar Gate carried rows of them in moulded glazed brick, alternating with bulls of Adad, and the reconstructed gate in Berlin is how most people have ever seen anything from Babylon. Older translations call it the sirrush, a misreading of the Akkadian that persisted long enough to attract attention from people hoping it was a surviving dinosaur.
entities.variantTraditions: The reading sirrush comes from a misdivision of the cuneiform and is obsolete, though it survives in older popular literature.

entities.name: Lamashtu
entities.role: The demon who kills infants and mothers in childbirth
symbols: a lion's head on a woman's body
entities.bio: A daughter of Anu who acts entirely on her own account, blamed for the deaths of newborns and of women in labour.
entities.longBio: Lamashtu is unusual among Mesopotamian demons: most act on orders, but she is a god's daughter who does harm because she wants to. She is shown with a lion's head, a hairy body, taloned feet like a bird's, holding snakes and suckling a piglet and a puppy at her breasts. She slips into the house, touches the woman's belly seven times, and takes the child. Every reality of neonatal and maternal death in the ancient world is gathered under her name. Protection against her was a serious industry - amulets, incantations, and above all the placing of a plaque or figurine of a second demon, Pazuzu, whose own ugliness was thought to drive her back to the marshes. Read as social history rather than theology, the Lamashtu material is a record of what people were most frightened of, and it was not war or famine.
entities.variantTraditions: The standard Lamashtu amulet shows her being driven down to the river on a donkey, with Pazuzu's head projecting over the top of the plaque as if peering over a wall.

entities.name: Pazuzu
entities.role: King of the wind demons, invoked for protection against Lamashtu
entities.abode: The wind out of the desert
entities.bio: A demon of the plague-bearing wind, kept in the house on purpose because he was worse than what he kept out.
entities.longBio: Pazuzu brings the hot dry wind out of the south-west, and with it fever and locusts - he is not benign. But he is set against Lamashtu, and the practical logic of Mesopotamian apotropaic magic is that you deploy the demon you can bargain with against the one you cannot. Small bronze heads of him were hung in doorways and over the beds of pregnant women, and his inscription has him announce that he came up and the wind blew and he turned it back. His head is dog-like or leonine, his body scaled, he has four wings and a raised right hand, and he is one of the few figures from this world with a genuine modern afterlife: the statue that appears in The Exorcist is a Pazuzu, which has made him easily the most famous Mesopotamian demon and given him a reputation as an arch-devil that the sources do not support.
entities.variantTraditions: Pazuzu is never described as an adversary of the gods or a ruler of hell; that role is entirely a twentieth-century invention.

entities.name: The Galla
entities.role: The demons who drag the living down to the underworld
domains: the enforcement of the underworld's claim
entities.bio: Underworld bailiffs who cannot be bribed, distracted, fed or reasoned with, sent to collect what is owed.
entities.longBio: The galla accompany Inanna back from the dead to make sure a substitute is delivered, and the poem describes them precisely by what they lack: they know no food, they know no drink, they eat no offering, they drink no libation, they accept no gift, they take no bribe. They do not enjoy a wife's embrace, they never kiss a child. Everything that could be used to influence a person is listed and denied. They are not cruel, they are simply not reachable - which is a more unsettling idea of death's agents than a torturing devil, and the text seems to know that too. They chase Dumuzi across the steppe, follow him through every transformation Utu grants him, and take him in the end.
entities.variantTraditions: Gallu passed into Akkadian as a general term for a class of demon, and the word has sometimes been connected, on thin evidence, with the Greek gello.

entities.name: Lilitu
entities.role: A night demon of the wind, ancestral to the later Lilith
entities.bio: One of a class of wind demons who visit sleepers, and the distant origin of a figure who became far more famous later.
entities.longBio: Lilitu belongs to a set of three related demons - lilu, lilitu and ardat lili - associated with the wind, the night and unmarried death. They are said to come to sleeping men and women, and to be dangerous to pregnant women and infants, functions overlapping with Lamashtu. The Mesopotamian evidence for them is real but thin, mostly incantation formulae. Everything that makes Lilith interesting - the first wife of Adam, the refusal to lie beneath him, the flight from Eden - comes from very much later Jewish material, principally the medieval Alphabet of Ben Sira, and cannot be read back into the cuneiform record. The famous Burney Relief was for decades described as Lilith on the basis of an early and now-abandoned identification.
entities.variantTraditions: The Burney Relief in the British Museum is now generally identified as Ishtar or Ereshkigal rather than Lilith, and the museum's own label has changed accordingly.

entities.name: The Apkallu
entities.role: The seven sages who brought the arts of civilisation before the flood
epithets: they who completed the plans of heaven and earth
symbols: the wings of the bird-headed genie
entities.bio: Seven sages sent by Enki out of the waters to teach humanity everything it needed, one to each of the antediluvian kings.
entities.longBio: The apkallu are Enki's emissaries, sent up from the Apsu to give the first cities the arts they had no way of inventing - writing, building, law, the crafts. The first and greatest, Adapa, served at Eridu. They are shown two ways in the art: as bearded men wearing a carp-skin cloak with the fish head as a hood, and as bird-headed winged figures holding a bucket and a cone, engaged in a purification gesture that appears on palace reliefs across Assyria. Berossus, writing in Greek in the third century BC, describes the first of them as Oannes, a being who emerged from the sea daily to teach and returned at night, and that account is the route by which the tradition reached later readers. After the flood the sages are succeeded by human scholars, and the whole scheme sets learning in the pre-flood age, which is why later scribes claimed antediluvian authority for their texts.
entities.variantTraditions: Berossus survives only in quotations by later authors, which makes his testimony valuable and unreliable in equal measure.

entities.name: Adapa
entities.role: The first sage, who broke the south wind's wing and refused the bread of life
epithets: he who broke the wing of the wind
entities.bio: A sage who was offered immortality and turned it down, because his own god had warned him it was poison.
entities.longBio: Adapa is fishing when the south wind capsizes his boat, and in his anger he curses it and breaks its wing, so that for seven days the wind does not blow. Anu summons him to answer for it. Ea coaches him: wear mourning, flatter the doorkeepers Dumuzi and Ningishzida, and above all, when they offer you bread and water, refuse them, because they are the bread and water of death. Adapa does exactly as told. But the gods, impressed by him and by the intercession of the two gatekeepers, offer him the bread and water of life instead - and he refuses, as instructed, and so refuses immortality. Anu laughs at him and sends him home. Whether Ea meant to protect him or to keep him mortal is the question the poem leaves open, and it is old, hard and unresolved: the wisest man alive is undone by obedience to the god of wisdom.
entities.variantTraditions: The story is often compared with Genesis 3 as an account of humanity losing immortality through eating or not eating; the parallel is suggestive but the mechanics are inverted.

entities.name: Atrahasis
entities.role: The exceedingly wise; the man who was warned and built the boat
entities.abode: Shuruppak, and afterwards at the mouth of the rivers
entities.bio: The man Enki warned through a reed wall, who built a boat, survived the flood, and was made immortal for it.
entities.longBio: The flood story survives in three related versions and this entry holds all of them. In Atrahasis the gods send plague, drought and famine to reduce a human population whose noise keeps Enlil awake, and each time Enki tells Atrahasis how to survive; when they resolve on a flood and bind themselves by oath not to warn anyone, Enki speaks his warning to a reed wall while Atrahasis is behind it. He builds a boat, loads it, and rides out seven days of storm during which the gods themselves are terrified and Ishtar cries out that she has destroyed her own people. Afterwards they are so hungry for offerings that they gather round his sacrifice like flies. In the Sumerian version he is Ziusudra; in the Gilgamesh epic he is Utnapishtim, and he is the one who tells Gilgamesh to his face that the immortality he is chasing was a one-time gift and will not be given again.
entities.variantTraditions: The parallels with Genesis - the boat, the birds released to test for land, the sacrifice after - are close enough that direct literary relationship is generally accepted, with the Mesopotamian version much the older.

entities.name: Gilgamesh
entities.role: King of Uruk; two-thirds god, who went looking for immortality and came home without it
symbols: the city wall of baked brick
entities.bio: The king who tyrannised his city, found the one friend who could match him, lost him, and went to the end of the world to argue with death.
entities.longBio: Gilgamesh begins as a bad king: he takes what he wants in Uruk until the people complain to the gods, who make Enkidu to be his equal. They fight, become inseparable, and go looking for glory - killing Humbaba in the Cedar Forest and the Bull of Heaven at Uruk. The gods condemn Enkidu for it, and he dies slowly and in terror over twelve days. That is the hinge of the poem. Gilgamesh, who has never been afraid of anything, refuses to bury him until a maggot falls from his nose, then puts on skins and goes out into the wilderness looking for a way not to die. He crosses the waters of death to Utnapishtim, fails a test of staying awake for a week, is given a rejuvenating plant as a consolation and has it stolen by a snake while he bathes. He comes home with nothing, and the poem ends where it began, with him showing off the walls of his city - the only thing that will outlast him.
entities.variantTraditions: Bilgames is the Sumerian form. He appears in the Sumerian King List with a reign of 126 years, and a historical king of that name in Early Dynastic Uruk is plausible but not proven.

entities.name: Enkidu
entities.role: The wild man made from clay to match Gilgamesh; his friend, and the first to die
epithets: he who was born in the steppe
entities.bio: Made by a goddess out of pinched clay to be Gilgamesh's match, civilised by a woman, and killed by the gods for the killings he took part in.
entities.longBio: Aruru washes her hands, pinches off clay, and throws it into the wilderness: Enkidu is born hairy, running with the gazelles, filling in the hunters' pits. He is brought into human life by Shamhat, who stays with him seven days, after which the animals will no longer have him and he finds he can think. He learns bread and beer, and goes to Uruk to stop the king from taking a bride. They wrestle to a standstill and love each other from that moment. His death is the most honest thing in the poem - a fever, twelve days, and a man who says plainly that he is afraid and that he wishes he had died in battle instead of like this. He curses Shamhat for civilising him, then, told by Shamash that she gave him bread, friendship and a king who will mourn him, takes the curse back. His dying dream of the house of dust is the fullest description of the Mesopotamian afterlife anywhere.
entities.variantTraditions: In the older Sumerian poems Enkidu is Gilgamesh's servant rather than his equal. The Akkadian epic promotes him to friend, which is the change that makes the story work.

entities.name: Shamhat
entities.role: The temple woman who made Enkidu human
epithets: she who civilised the wild man
entities.bio: Sent to the waterhole to meet a wild man, she gave him language, clothing and grief, and he cursed her and then blessed her for it.
entities.longBio: A trapper finds his pits filled in and his traps sprung by something that runs with the herd, and is advised to bring Shamhat, a woman of Ishtar's temple, to the watering place. She waits, opens her robe, and stays with Enkidu six days and seven nights. Afterwards the gazelles run from him and he cannot keep up; his body has weakened and his mind has grown. She teaches him to wear cloth, to eat bread, to drink beer until he is cheerful, and takes him to the city. The poem treats what she does as the making of a human being, without irony and without shame - the sexual encounter is the mechanism of civilisation rather than a fall from it, which is a genuinely different account of the same materials that Genesis handles very differently. Dying, Enkidu curses her, and Shamash reminds him what she gave him, and he blesses her instead.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether the temple women of Ishtar practised anything that can accurately be called sacred prostitution is now heavily disputed; the older scholarly picture, drawn largely from Herodotus, has not held up well.

entities.name: Siduri
entities.role: The alewife at the edge of the world, who told Gilgamesh to go home
domains: the tavern at the world's edge
entities.abode: By the shore of the waters of death
entities.bio: The divine tavern-keeper who bars her door against a filthy stranger, then gives him the best advice in the poem, which he ignores.
entities.longBio: Gilgamesh arrives at Siduri's tavern at the edge of the world in animal skins, hollow-cheeked, and she takes him for a killer and bolts the door. He explains himself and she lets him in, and then in the Old Babylonian version she says the thing everyone remembers: that the life he is looking for he will not find, because when the gods made humanity they kept life for themselves and allotted death to people - so fill your belly, be happy day and night, dance and play, wash and put on clean clothes, look at the child who holds your hand, and let your wife delight in your embrace. It is the oldest surviving statement of that argument, and it is put in the mouth of a woman running a bar. Gilgamesh does not take it. He asks her the way across the water instead, and she tells him where to find the ferryman.
entities.variantTraditions: This speech is present in the Old Babylonian version and absent from the later Standard Babylonian recension, which drops it. Its resemblance to Ecclesiastes 9 has been much discussed.

entities.name: Urshanabi
entities.role: The ferryman who crosses the waters of death
domains: the crossing of the waters of death
entities.bio: Utnapishtim's ferryman, whose stone crew Gilgamesh destroyed before realising he needed them.
entities.longBio: Urshanabi crews his boat with the stone ones, which allow it to cross water that kills anything living that touches it. Gilgamesh, arriving in a temper, smashes them - and so has to be told to go and cut three hundred punting poles, using each once and letting it go so his hand never touches the water. It is a nicely judged detail: the hero's habit of destroying whatever is in front of him creates the obstacle he then has to labour through. Afterwards Urshanabi is dismissed from Utnapishtim's service for having brought a stranger, and goes back to Uruk with Gilgamesh, where the last lines of the epic have Gilgamesh showing him the city walls - the boatman of the dead as the audience for a speech about what a man leaves behind.
entities.variantTraditions: The stone ones are obscure; readings range from stone figurines that propel the boat to a crew of stone giants, and the text does not settle it.

entities.name: Ninsun
entities.role: The wild cow; Gilgamesh's divine mother, who reads his dreams
entities.bio: A goddess married to a mortal king, who interprets her son's dreams correctly and adopts his friend to protect him.
entities.longBio: Ninsun is Gilgamesh's mother by Lugalbanda, which is where his two-thirds divinity comes from. Her role in the epic is that of a mother who understands exactly what is happening and cannot stop it. Gilgamesh brings her two dreams - a falling star and an axe, both of which he is drawn to as to a wife - and she reads them at once: a companion is coming, strong as the stars of heaven, whom you will love. When the two set out for the Cedar Forest she goes up to the roof, burns incense, and complains to Shamash directly for having given her son a restless heart. Then she adopts Enkidu as her own son so that he will have a family and a claim on the gods. It does not save him. She is one of the very few characters in the literature who behaves purely well and is not rewarded for it.
entities.variantTraditions: In the Sumerian poems she is the wife of Lugalbanda and mother of Gilgamesh already; the epic inherits rather than invents the relationship.

entities.name: Lugalbanda
entities.role: King of Uruk; Gilgamesh's father, abandoned sick in the mountains and befriended by the Anzu bird
entities.abode: Uruk, and the mountains of Zabu
entities.bio: Left for dead in a mountain cave on campaign, he survived, won the Anzu bird's favour, and ran faster than an army.
entities.longBio: Lugalbanda's two Sumerian poems are among the best-told narratives in the corpus and are not much known outside the field. On campaign against Aratta he falls ill, and his brothers, unable to carry him and unwilling to abandon him unprovisioned, leave him in a cave with food and his weapons, intending to collect his body on the way back. He recovers alone, prays to the sun, the moon and Inanna, and survives in the wilderness. Then he finds the nest of the Anzu bird, feeds and decorates its chick while the parents are away, and the returning Anzu - delighted rather than enraged - grants him a gift. He asks for speed, and gets the power to run without tiring, which lets him rejoin the army, cross back alone to Uruk for Inanna's counsel, and return. He is later listed as a king of Uruk and deified.
entities.variantTraditions: The Sumerian King List gives him a reign of 1200 years. That he was an actual early ruler of Uruk is possible; the poems are literary compositions of much later date.

entities.name: Enmerkar
entities.role: King of Uruk who is credited with the invention of writing
domains: the invention of the written message
entities.bio: In a long-distance quarrel with a rival city, he wrote his message down because his messenger could not memorise it - and so, the poem says, invented writing.
entities.longBio: Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta is a story about a trade dispute conducted by envoy over enormous distances, each side sending riddles and demands. At one point the message is so long that the messenger's mouth is too heavy and he cannot repeat it, so Enmerkar patted clay and set the words on it as on a tablet - and the poem states plainly that before that day no one had ever put words on clay. It is an origin story for writing told by the people who used it, and its explanation is thoroughly practical: the message got too long to carry in a person's head. The same composition contains a passage about a time when all peoples spoke to Enlil in a single tongue, and how that was changed - which has been compared with Babel often enough to have its own literature.
entities.variantTraditions: The Babel comparison rests on a difficult passage that has been translated in opposite senses - as the confusing of a single language or the ending of a rivalry between two. Neither reading is secure.

entities.name: Etana
entities.role: The shepherd king who flew to heaven on an eagle to find the plant of birth
epithets: the shepherd who ascended to heaven
symbols: the shrinking earth seen from above
entities.bio: A king with no heir who rescued a maimed eagle and was carried up toward heaven to fetch the plant of birth.
entities.longBio: Etana's problem is ordinary: he has no son. The poem is framed by a fable - an eagle and a snake swear friendship over a tree, the eagle eats the snake's young, and the snake, advised by Shamash, hides in a carcass and catches the eagle, tearing off its wings and throwing it into a pit. Etana finds it there, feeds it back to health, and asks in return to be carried to heaven where the plant of birth grows. They fly, and the poem describes the earth receding at each league until the sea looks like a gardener's ditch - one of the earliest imagined views of the world from above. Then the tablets break. Whether he reached it and fell, or reached it and succeeded, is unknown, though the King List gives him a successor named Balih, which suggests he got what he came for.
entities.variantTraditions: The ending is genuinely lost rather than ambiguous. Older accounts that describe Etana falling are extrapolating from the flight scene, not reporting a text.

entities.name: Sargon of Akkad
entities.role: Founder of the Akkadian empire, set adrift as a baby in a reed basket
symbols: the reed basket sealed with bitumen
entities.bio: A real emperor with a legendary birth: born in secret, sealed in a basket of reeds, drawn from the river and raised as a gardener.
entities.longBio: Sargon is historical - he unified Sumer and Akkad around 2334 BC, built the first empire the region had seen, installed his daughter Enheduanna as high priestess at Ur, and founded a dynasty that lasted a century and a half. The legend attached to him is what belongs in a mythology. In his own words, his mother was a high priestess who conceived him in secret, bore him in hiding, set him in a basket of rushes sealed with bitumen and put him in the river; Akki the water-drawer found him, raised him as a gardener, and Ishtar loved him and gave him kingship. The correspondence with the infancy of Moses is close and has been argued over for a century and a half. The Sargon text as we have it is Neo-Assyrian, written well over a millennium after him, and is best understood as a legitimation story for later kings.
entities.variantTraditions: The surviving Birth Legend is far later than Sargon himself. Whether it influenced the Moses account, drew on shared regional convention, or is independent, is not settled.

entities.name: Naram-Sin
entities.role: Sargon's grandson, who called himself a god and was blamed for the fall of Akkad
entities.bio: The first Mesopotamian king to write himself as a god, and the villain of a poem that blames him for his empire's destruction.
entities.longBio: Naram-Sin was a successful and self-confident emperor who took the title king of the four quarters and, unprecedentedly, had the divine determinative written before his name - his victory stele shows him climbing a mountain over his enemies, wearing the horned helmet that marks a god. The Curse of Agade, composed after his dynasty fell, tells it differently: denied a favourable omen for rebuilding Enlil's temple at Nippur, he waited seven years, then took an axe to the Ekur himself, and Enlil answered by bringing down the Gutians from the mountains, a people described as not classed among people. The city of Akkad was destroyed so thoroughly that its site has still not been located. Whether the poem is theology or hindsight, it is one of the earliest surviving arguments that a state fell because its ruler offended a god.
entities.variantTraditions: Modern historians attribute the collapse of Akkad chiefly to a severe regional drought around 2200 BC, evidenced in soil cores; the Curse of Agade is a theological reading of a climatic event.

entities.name: Hammurabi
entities.role: King of Babylon, who received his laws from the sun god
domains: the raising of Babylon and of Marduk
symbols: the rod and ring received from Shamash
entities.bio: The king whose law code is carved beneath an image of him receiving authority from Shamash, and under whom Marduk rose.
entities.longBio: Hammurabi's stele is a genuinely arresting object: nearly two and a quarter metres of black diorite, with a relief at the top showing the king standing before the seated Shamash, who holds out the rod and the ring - the measuring tools that signify just rule. Below it, in almost three hundred provisions, is the law. It is not the earliest code, Ur-Nammu's is older, and it is more a royal monument than a working statute book, but it is the fullest. Its prologue and epilogue are theology: Anu and Enlil called Marduk to supremacy and Hammurabi to govern for him, so that the strong should not oppress the weak. The stele was carried off to Susa as loot in the twelfth century BC and found there in 1901, which is why it survived. Under his reign Babylon became the political and religious centre, and Marduk's promotion followed.
entities.variantTraditions: The famous eye for an eye provisions apply differently by social class, and the code's relationship to actual court practice is much debated.

entities.name: Enheduanna
entities.role: High priestess of Nanna at Ur; the earliest author known by name
entities.bio: Sargon's daughter, high priestess at Ur, and the first person anywhere to put a name to written work.
entities.longBio: Enheduanna was installed by her father Sargon as high priestess of the moon god at Ur, an office that combined religious authority with the political business of holding conquered Sumer together. She composed - and signed - a body of hymns, principally the Exaltation of Inanna, in which she describes being driven out of her office during a rebellion, exiled, and appealing to Inanna to restore her. She names herself in the text and speaks in the first person about her own suffering and her own composition, which is why she is generally called the earliest known author. Her temple hymns were copied by scribes for centuries after her death. A limestone disc bearing her name and image was excavated at Ur in the 1920s, deliberately broken in antiquity and then buried.
entities.variantTraditions: The attribution has been questioned: some scholars argue the hymns are later compositions written in her voice. The majority position still treats her as a real author, and the debate is live.

entities.name: Ashurbanipal
entities.role: The last great Assyrian king, who could read, and who collected the library
epithets: he who reads the tablets before the flood
domains: the collecting of every text that could be found
entities.bio: A literate emperor who sent agents to strip the temple archives of Babylonia, and so preserved most of what we can read today.
entities.longBio: Almost everything in this pack comes down to us because of one man's collecting habit. Ashurbanipal was unusual among Assyrian kings in being trained as a scribe, and boasted of it - he claimed to read the obscure Sumerian and the difficult Akkadian, and to understand the tablets from before the flood. He had agents comb the temple libraries of Babylonia for anything not already in his collection, copying or confiscating. The result was some thirty thousand tablets at Nineveh, systematically organised. When the city was sacked in 612 BC the burning building fired the clay and preserved it. Excavated from the 1850s, this is the library that gave the world the Enuma Elish, the standard Gilgamesh, the omen series and the medical corpus. He also had the lion-hunt reliefs carved, which are among the finest things any Assyrian workshop produced.
entities.variantTraditions: The library is not entirely his: it incorporates earlier royal collections, and material continued to be added under his successors.

entities.name: Ishum
entities.role: Herald of Erra; the restraining voice beside the god of slaughter
domains: fire as a lamp rather than a burning
entities.bio: The counsellor who walks in front of the plague god and talks him down after the city is already ruined.
entities.longBio: Ishum's whole function is to be the voice of restraint next to a god who does not have any. In Erra and Ishum, Erra is roused to slaughter, and Ishum argues with him at every stage - first trying to prevent it, then, when Babylon has already been emptied, persuading him to stop and to bless what is left. The poem was popular enough that copies were hung in houses as protective amulets, on the logic that the text in which Erra is calmed will keep him calm. Ishum is also a benign fire god, the torch that goes ahead of a procession and the watchman who walks the streets at night - fire as safety rather than destruction, which is exactly the counterweight the pairing needs.
entities.variantTraditions: Ishum is identified with the Sumerian Hendursaga, the herald god, and the equation is made explicitly in god-lists.

entities.name: Bau
entities.role: Lady of Lagash; healing goddess and wife of Ningirsu
epithets: she who gives life to the dead
entities.abode: Girsu, in the state of Lagash
entities.bio: The healing goddess of Lagash, whose marriage to the city god was the great annual festival there.
entities.longBio: Bau is the principal goddess of Lagash, a city-state that has left us more administrative documentation than almost anywhere else in early Mesopotamia - the archive of her temple household records the rations, personnel and landholdings of an institution employing well over a thousand people, and it is one of the best windows we have onto how a temple economy actually worked. Her marriage to Ningirsu was celebrated at the New Year with the presentation of gifts. Like Gula she is a healer and is associated with dogs, and in the later periods the two goddesses are largely conflated. Gudea's cylinders, the longest Sumerian literary text on a single object, describe the building of her husband's temple in extraordinary detail, down to the making of the first brick.
entities.variantTraditions: The reading of the name is uncertain: Bau, Baba and Bawu all appear in the literature, with Baba currently preferred by many Assyriologists.

entities.name: Ninazu
entities.role: Lord physician; an underworld god of healing and snakes
entities.bio: A god who is both a healer and a lord of the dead, which is less of a contradiction here than it looks.
entities.longBio: Ninazu's name means lord physician, and he belongs to the underworld - the two go together because the same power that can call a body back from illness is the power that governs where bodies go. He is the father of Ningishzida and shares his serpent associations; the mushussu dragon was his emblem before it passed to Tishpak and eventually to Marduk, following the political fortunes of Eshnunna. In the Sumerian composition Ninazu and Ninmada he is involved in bringing barley down from heaven to the land. His cult at Eshnunna was displaced when the city changed hands, and the transfer of his dragon to the incoming god is one of the clearest examples of an emblem outliving the deity who owned it.
entities.variantTraditions: There appear to have been two distinct traditions of Ninazu, one at Eshnunna in the north and one at Enegi in the south, later treated as one god.

entities.name: Nanaya
entities.role: Goddess of love and desire, closely linked to Inanna but distinct from her
entities.bio: A love goddess of Uruk who kept a separate cult from Inanna for two thousand years despite constantly being confused with her.
entities.longBio: Nanaya is one of the most persistently popular goddesses in the record and one of the least discussed outside the field. She overlaps with Inanna so much that god-lists sometimes treat her as an aspect, but she held her own temples, her own festivals and her own priesthood from the Ur III period into the Parthian era - a span of well over two thousand years. Her hymns are frankly erotic and often in the first person, praising her own attractions. She was worshipped at Uruk alongside Inanna, later at Borsippa alongside Nabu, and her cult travelled unusually far, appearing in Elam, in Egypt among Aramaic-speaking communities, and eventually in Palmyra. The love goddess who is not Ishtar is a useful corrective to the habit of reducing every such figure to one.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether Nanaya began as a hypostasis of Inanna that acquired independence, or as a separate goddess drawn into her orbit, is not resolved.

entities.name: Ishtaran
entities.role: Divine judge of Der; settler of border disputes
entities.abode: Der, on the road to Elam
entities.bio: The god of a frontier city, called in to arbitrate the longest-running border dispute in recorded history.
entities.longBio: Ishtaran presided at Der, a city on the frontier between Mesopotamia and Elam, and his speciality was the settlement of boundaries - which is what a frontier god would be good for. He is invoked in the famous dispute between Lagash and Umma over the Gu-edin, a stretch of irrigated farmland the two city-states fought over intermittently for something like a hundred and fifty years, in what is the earliest border conflict for which we have documentation from both sides. His minister is the serpent god Nirah, and Ishtaran himself has serpent associations, though the reason is unclear. A boundary god with a snake for a herald, in a city that spent its existence between two empires, is a neat piece of local theology.
entities.variantTraditions: Some texts appear to describe Ishtaran dying or being in the underworld, which has been read as a dying-god motif; the passages are obscure and the reading is contested.

entities.name: Zababa
entities.role: War god of Kish; the eagle-standard of the battle line
entities.bio: The war god of Kish, whose name gave its authority to a title claimed by kings for two thousand years.
entities.longBio: Zababa is the city god of Kish, and Kish mattered out of proportion to its size: the title king of Kish was claimed by rulers all over Mesopotamia long after the city itself had ceased to be important, because it carried a sense of legitimate overlordship. Zababa is a war god pure and simple, identified with Ninurta in the later god-lists and given Bau or Ishtar as consort depending on the period. His emblem is an eagle-headed staff. Hammurabi's law stele mentions the restoration of his temple, and the Kassite kings kept up his cult. He is a good example of a deity whose importance is entirely a function of his city's prestige - the theology never developed much, but the name stayed useful.
entities.variantTraditions: Zababa is thoroughly identified with Ninurta in first-millennium sources, to the point where the two are hard to separate.

entities.name: Lugal-irra and Meslamta-ea
entities.role: Divine twins who stand at the gate of the underworld
symbols: a pair of identical figures with axe and mace
entities.abode: The doorway, and the gate below
entities.bio: Identical twin gods buried in figurine pairs at either side of a door, and the constellation we still call the Twins.
entities.longBio: Lugal-irra and Meslamta-ea are always a pair and are functionally one entry. Small figurines of them were buried at the two sides of a doorway, one on the left and one on the right, to keep out anything harmful - a piece of household practice attested by both the ritual texts and the excavated figurines. They belong to the underworld, and both are associated with Nergal, Meslamta-ea being effectively a name of his. In the sky they are the constellation MUL.MASH.TAB.BA.GAL.GAL, the Great Twins, which is the constellation the Greeks received as Gemini and which is still called the Twins in every European language. The stars changed hands; the idea of a pair standing together did not.
entities.variantTraditions: Meslamta-ea means he who comes forth from the Meslam, Nergal's temple at Kutha, and the two figures are sometimes treated as aspects of Nergal rather than separate gods.

entities.name: The Scorpion-Men
entities.role: Scorpion people who guard the mountain gate where the sun rises
symbols: a human torso on a scorpion's body
entities.abode: Mount Mashu, at the edge of the world
entities.bio: Terrifying gate-guards who question Gilgamesh at the mountain of the sunrise and, unexpectedly, let him through.
entities.longBio: At the twin mountain of Mashu, whose peaks reach to heaven and whose base reaches to the underworld, the gate through which the sun passes is guarded by scorpion-men, described as so dreadful that their aura is death and the sight of them fatal. Gilgamesh covers his face and approaches anyway. What follows is a good example of how this literature undercuts expectation: they interrogate him, recognise that he is two-thirds god, warn him that the passage is twelve leagues of total darkness that no one has ever walked, and then open the gate. He runs the tunnel in the dark, feeling the wind at his back, and emerges into a garden of jewelled trees. The guardians are not an obstacle to be killed - they are the last people to give him honest advice before the world ends.
entities.variantTraditions: Scorpion-men appear in Mesopotamian art from the third millennium and were among the eleven monsters Tiamat created, which the Gilgamesh passage does not mention.

entities.name: Ur-Nammu
entities.role: King of Ur; builder of the great ziggurat and author of the oldest surviving law code
symbols: the builder's basket carried on the head
entities.bio: The king who wrote laws three centuries before Hammurabi and built the ziggurat that still stands.
entities.longBio: Ur-Nammu founded the Third Dynasty of Ur and left two things behind. The first is the ziggurat at Ur, the best preserved in Mesopotamia, its lower stage still standing after four thousand years and heavily restored in the twentieth century. His foundation inscriptions and the famous stele showing him carrying a builder's basket on his head - the king as labourer for the god - come from that programme. The second is the law code that bears his name, roughly three centuries older than Hammurabi's and the earliest surviving anywhere. It is notably less brutal: where Hammurabi prescribes bodily retaliation, Ur-Nammu's provisions mostly require monetary compensation for injury. A composition called The Death of Ur-Nammu describes him dying in battle and arriving in the underworld with gifts for its officials.
entities.variantTraditions: The code may have been issued by his son Shulgi rather than by him; the attribution is disputed on the basis of the prologue.

entities.name: Shulgi
entities.role: King of Ur who declared himself a god and boasted of being able to read
epithets: he who is skilled in the tablet
entities.bio: An administrator-king who had himself worshipped as a god and left hymns advertising his own literacy and athleticism.
entities.longBio: Shulgi ruled for nearly half a century and reorganised the state with a thoroughness that shows in the archives - standardised weights and measures, a recalibrated calendar, a bookkeeping system so detailed that tens of thousands of its tablets survive, and a road network with rest houses. He also had himself deified during his own lifetime and his praise-hymns composed and copied in the scribal schools, which had the effect of making his self-promotion part of the curriculum. Those hymns are extraordinary documents of royal self-regard: he claims to read and write like a scribe, to know Sumerian, Akkadian, Elamite and Amorite, to be a skilled musician, and to have run from Nippur to Ur and back in a single day through a storm to celebrate festivals in both cities.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether the Ur III kings were worshipped as gods in the full sense, or honoured with divine trappings as a political device, is a long-running argument.

entities.name: Gudea
entities.role: Ruler of Lagash; temple builder, known from more statues than any other Mesopotamian
symbols: the seated statue with the temple plan on the lap
entities.bio: A ruler who built a temple on the instructions of a dream, and recorded the whole process on two clay cylinders.
entities.longBio: Gudea governed Lagash in the period between the fall of Akkad and the rise of Ur III, and left an unusually complete record of a single religious act. The two Gudea Cylinders - the longest Sumerian literary composition on any single object - describe how he received a dream he could not interpret, took it to the dream-goddess Nanshe, and was told that Ningirsu wanted his temple, the Eninnu, rebuilt. What follows covers the purification of the city, the sourcing of cedar and diorite and gold from as far as the Amanus and the Gulf, the making of the first brick in its mould, the seven-day festival, and the god's installation. He is also the best-portrayed individual from ancient Mesopotamia: more than two dozen of his statues in hard diorite survive, several showing him seated with an architectural plan across his knees.
entities.variantTraditions: Gudea's inscriptions are notably free of military boasting, which is unusual and has been read both as genuine piety and as the posture available to a small state between empires.

entities.name: Mamitu
entities.role: The sworn oath personified; goddess of binding curses
epithets: the curse of the broken word
entities.bio: The oath itself, made into a goddess, who comes after anyone who swears falsely.
entities.longBio: Mamitu is the Akkadian word for an oath, and also a goddess - the distinction between a binding formula and a divine being is not one this culture drew sharply. When two parties swore, the oath became an entity with a claim on them, and if it was broken the mamitu was what came. Much of the medical and exorcistic literature is concerned with diagnosing which oath a sick person has unknowingly violated, since illness was frequently understood as the working out of a curse rather than as a physical process. She sits among the judges of the underworld in some texts and is listed as a consort of Nergal in others. She is a good illustration of how much of this religion was contractual: the spoken word, once given, was an object with power of its own.
entities.variantTraditions: The same word covers the oath, the curse that enforces it, and the goddess, and translators must choose between them line by line.
